title: Superbad
logline: Two high-school seniors try to buy alcohol for a party. Raunchy, dialogue-driven teen comedy with a cop subplot.
overview: Two co-dependent high school seniors are forced to deal with separation anxiety after their plan to stage a booze-soaked party goes awry.

jokes.text: 'The Vag-tastic Voyage' — the name of the porn website, delivered deadpan
jokes.setup: Seth is describing the website he wants to subscribe to
jokes.punchline: The name is a pun on 'Fantastic Voyage,' delivered with zero self-consciousness
jokes.explanation: A punchy, quotable portmanteau that doubles as a movie reference. The name is funny on its own, and even funnier that Seth says it with the confidence of someone citing a blue-chip investment. The economy is near-perfect — three words do all the work.

jokes.text: 'That's disgusting. You're like an animal.' / 'I'm normal as shit. Peeing on people. That's normal?'
jokes.setup: Evan calls Seth disgusting for browsing fetish content that 'comes with the site'
jokes.punchline: Seth reframes fetish content as normal while simultaneously confirming he has at least considered the pee fetish
jokes.explanation: Classic Seth logic: aggressive defensiveness where the defense inadvertently confirms the accusation. 'I'm normal as shit' is a great character line. The rhythm of Evan's callback — 'Peeing on people. That's normal?' — is well-timed and efficient.

jokes.text: "You're weird for not liking porn. I'm normal as shit."
jokes.setup: Evan calls Seth disgusting for his porn tastes
jokes.punchline: Seth reframes himself as the normal one and Evan as the deviant, delivered with complete conviction
jokes.explanation: Economical and sharp. The aggressor-as-victim flip ('I'm normal as shit') is a classic Seth move — he genuinely believes this — and the casual 'as shit' intensifier on 'normal' is a perfect comic collision. High quotability.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, well, I'm sorry the Coen Brothers don't direct the porn that I watch. They're hard to get ahold of, okay?'
jokes.setup: Seth complains about wanting 'production value' — editing, transitions, music — in porn
jokes.punchline: Evan sarcastically invokes the Coen Brothers, then Seth plays it completely straight
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. Evan's sarcastic jab ('I'm sorry the Coen Brothers don't direct the porn I watch') is sharp and quotable on its own — an absurdist high-low collision. But Seth's follow-up ('They're hard to get ahold of, okay?') elevates it into something exceptional: he takes the absurd premise completely seriously, confirming he has apparently considered it. The structure is perfect — sarcasm met with sincerity creates maximum comedic dissonance. Highly quotable, strong craft.

jokes.text: 'You probably should pick the one with the least dirty name.' / 'What about Perfect Ten? Because that could be a bowling website.'
jokes.setup: Evan points out Seth's parents will see the billing name
jokes.punchline: Seth's criteria for pornography is now plausible deniability; he proposes 'Perfect Ten' because 'that could be a bowling website'
jokes.explanation: The pivot from production-value connoisseur to cover-story strategist in one breath is very funny. The specificity of bowling as the alibi is a nice comic choice — it's the most wholesome possible alternative reading.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, but they don't really show dick going in, which is a huge concern.'
jokes.setup: Evan suggests 'Perfect Ten' as a reputable-sounding porn site
jokes.punchline: Seth has a very specific deal-breaker: insufficient penetration visibility. Delivered with the gravity of a product defect.
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'which is a huge concern' treats pornographic explicitness as a consumer-protection issue. The deadpan tone sells it completely. Very economical — the punchline is exactly as long as it needs to be.

jokes.text: Evan's flat 'I didn't realize that' — reaction beat to Seth's penetration-visibility dealbreaker
jokes.setup: Seth has just delivered an extremely specific porn complaint
jokes.punchline: Evan responds with the flattest possible acknowledgment, as if Seth just told him a mundane fact
jokes.explanation: Perfect straight-man economy. Evan's non-reaction is funnier than any comeback could be. Four words that communicate complete resignation to Seth's insanity.

jokes.text: 'Plus, have you ever seen a vagina by itself? Not for me.'
jokes.setup: Continuing the Perfect Ten discussion
jokes.punchline: Seth has an aesthetic preference against solo anatomy shots — delivered as a surprisingly relatable (if crude) personal taste
jokes.explanation: Brief but effective. The casualness of 'Not for me' — as if discussing a food preference — is the whole joke. Good economy.

jokes.text: Seth's mom (Jane) drops off the boys at school and Seth pretends not to know her / acts like he's not a piece of meat
jokes.setup: Seth's mom drives the boys to school with cheerful maternal energy moments after they were debating porn
jokes.punchline: The tonal whiplash from graphic pornography discussion to 'Hi! Thanks for taking him, Seth!' is the joke; Seth's embarrassed monosyllables complete it
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition comedy works (porn discussion → mom appears) but the execution doesn't push it far enough. 'I'm not a piece of meat' is odd but underdeveloped. The scene functions more as setup for the next joke.

jokes.text: 'I am truly jealous you got to suck on those tits when you were a baby.'
jokes.setup: Evan's attractive mom has just driven away. The boys are standing outside school.
jokes.punchline: Seth expresses genuine envy about infant breastfeeding — framed as a sincere deprivation he has contemplated
jokes.explanation: One of the standout jokes in the reel. The delivery is everything — 'truly jealous' and 'when you were a baby' are precise modifiers that make an already transgressive thought even funnier. The sincerity is what elevates it from shock humor to character comedy: Seth genuinely means this. It's also very quotable and captures the horny-idiot-with-a-heart-of-gold essence of his character perfectly. Economy is excellent — not a wasted word.

jokes.punchline: Evan's retort implies Seth's dad is gay and that Seth performed fellatio on him — a deliberately absurd and disproportionate comeback
jokes.explanation: It's a swing-back insult that earns points for surprise and willingness to go dark, but the logic doesn't quite track (it's a non sequitur). It gets a laugh more from shock than from craft. The 13-second gap [03:57 to 04:11] suggests the comedic silence/reaction lands visually.

jokes.explanation: 'Vagine' as a malapropism/deliberate mispronunciation is a Seth-specific verbal quirk that becomes a running element. The Red Bull justification is perfectly banal. Good character work.

jokes.explanation: Classic Seth grandiosity. The escalation from 'I'm about to graduate' to 'they owe me ball-sac service' is characteristically unhinged. 'Three years' is also a nice detail — implying he failed a year (or just can't count), which is a subtle extra layer.

jokes.explanation: The rhetorical uplift ('one day wanna live in') applied to something deeply unserious is a great comedic device. It's character-rich — Seth genuinely believes in this cause. Very quotable in context.

jokes.text: Seth's 'peak of my ass-getting career' speech — two dozen handjobs, three-quarters of a blowjob, calling himself 'Orson Welles'

The Orson Welles comparison is inspired: a 17-year-old applying the arc of a legendary filmmaker's career to his sexual history is perfectly absurd and yet internally coherent for Seth. 'Three-quarters of a blowjob' is an exquisitely specific number. And 'I honestly see now why Orson Welles ate his fat ass to death' as the capper is genuinely exceptional — it takes the metaphor to its grotesque logical conclusion. This is craft-level joke writing: original, well-structured, deeply character-specific, economical, and entirely earned.

jokes.text: Look, it was the peak of my ass-getting career, and it happened way too early.

jokes.punchline: Applying career-arc language ('peak,' 'too early') to a teenager's sex life — framing two dozen handjobs as a professional zenith he has never recovered from.
jokes.explanation: The professional-career framing applied to adolescent sexual history is a consistent Seth technique that works because he takes it entirely seriously. 'Ass-getting career' as a formal category is excellent.

Seth means it seriously but the construction is brilliantly crude — the phrase 'suck dick at' (meaning 'be bad at') crashing into 'fucking pussy' creates an absurd contradiction. It sounds like it was written by Seth himself, which is exactly right. Very quotable and much funnier on rewatch when you catch the structure.

jokes.explanation: A brilliant escalation of the Orson Welles bit. 'Ate his fat ass to death' is colorfully economical, the logic (why Welles ate himself to oblivion = why Seth might eat himself to oblivion after peaking with Shauna) is absurd but internally consistent, and the commitment to the metaphor is what makes it land. This is the kind of line that becomes a cultural reference within a friend group. Near top-of-reel quality.

jokes.text: Matt Muir is introduced as a threat — 'Have you ever stared into his eyes? It was like the first time I heard the Beatles.'

jokes.explanation: Genuinely funny and strange. Using the Beatles as the benchmark for a teenage boy's dreamy eyes is an unexpected and very specific choice. 'He's the sweetest guy ever' preceding the Beatle-eye revelation makes it funnier — Seth sounds like he might be in love with Matt Muir. The joke rewards the absurdity of Seth being threatened by sweetness rather than physical dominance.

jokes.text: Jesse disinvites Seth and Evan to his party to their faces, then Seth has to relay the message to Evan

jokes.explanation: 'Dive in front of his spit' is a good specific visual image — the bodyguard instinct applied to saliva. Evan's dry deflation of Seth's victimhood is well-executed.

jokes.explanation: More of a tonal/character beat than a joke, but the contrast of abstract math pedagogy and Seth's raw frustration is lightly comedic. The 'Pussy' mutter is funny in context. Not a standout.

jokes.text: Evan awkwardly tells Becca she can keep the pen she borrowed, in increasing detail: 'You won't have to borrow one again because you'll have that one.'
jokes.setup: Evan runs into Becca, his crush, in the hallway
jokes.punchline: His attempt at a smooth, casual interaction spirals into a detailed explanation of pen ownership logic
jokes.explanation: Classic awkward teenage boy overcommunicating to a crush. Evan's character — nervous, over-explaining, completely unable to play it cool — is established efficiently. The specificity of the pen logic is funny.

jokes.text: Evan lies to Becca about not being at Dimitri's party — improvising an increasingly elaborate alternative night involving 'adult conversations,' 'a man who claimed he had climbed five mountains,' and a nightclub
jokes.setup: Becca asks why she never sees Evan at parties
jokes.punchline: His cover story escalates from plausible ('had some friends over') to absurd ('talked to a man who claimed he had climbed five mountains') to impossible ('went to a nightclub')
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure is excellent. Each beat is more implausible than the last, and 'a man who claimed he had climbed five mountains in his life' is a specifically hilarious detail — the word 'claimed' implying Evan suspects the boast. The intercut with Seth's actual night (going to look at tits, nearly getting in a fight at a 'nightclub') is masterful visual comedy that elevates the joke. Evan's desperation to seem interesting to Becca is perfectly observed.

The juxtaposition of Evan's flowery language ('an incredible, unbelievable night') against Seth screaming 'Gonna look at tits right now!' and challenging a 'roid monkey' is a structurally elegant joke. The intercuts are brief and punchy. Calling the man a ''roid monkey' is also a funny specific insult.

jokes.text: Evan's fabricated story contains 'That's Vag-tastic!' — an accidental verbal slip while describing his cool Saturday night to Becca

jokes.explanation: A perfect callback. 'Vag-tastic' bleeding into Evan's carefully constructed cool-guy speech to his crush is funny on multiple levels: it reveals the morning's conversation is still rattling around his head, it's maximally inappropriate in context, and it's a great payoff to the opening joke. The fact that it passes unremarked makes it even better — Becca apparently doesn't notice or Evan powers through. Very rewatchable.

jokes.text: Seth rants to his Home Ec teacher that he joined the class expecting a partner and can't get 'twice the grades for doing all the work'
jokes.setup: Seth apparently signed up for Home Ec to coast with a partner who never shows up
jokes.punchline: His grievance about not getting 'twice the grades' reveals his entire strategy for the class — a lazy workaround that has now backfired
jokes.explanation: The teacher's flat 'I didn't invent odd numbers, Seth' is a perfect deadpan response to Seth's escalating complaint. Seth's argument that he deserves double grades for solo work is stupid-but-logical in a classic Seth way.

jokes.text: Mrs. Hayworth: 'I didn't invent odd numbers, Seth.'
jokes.setup: Seth has complained that it's unfair he has to work alone in Home Ec
jokes.punchline: The teacher deflects all accountability with the most economical possible non-answer
jokes.explanation: Six words that completely shut down Seth's whining. Perfect teacher-student comedic economy. The logic is watertight (she really didn't) while being completely unhelpful. Probably the best adult-character line in the reel.

jokes.text: Seth gestures toward Evan and his partner: 'Look at that. Looks like the most fun I've ever seen in my life. And it's B.S. Excuse my language.'
jokes.setup: Seth is making his case to the teacher for why his situation is unfair
jokes.punchline: His self-censoring 'excuse my language' after 'B.S.' — having previously said 'shitty' and 'fucking' — is an absurd gesture of selective propriety
jokes.explanation: The self-aware 'excuse my language' after a torrent of profanity is a good irony beat. Seth's uneven self-regulation is very consistent with his character.

jokes.text: Seth: 'I'm like a single mother.'
jokes.setup: Seth has been describing how he has to do all the cooking himself — washing and drying
jokes.punchline: He compares his situation in Home Ec to being a single mother — an escalation that reframes high school cooking class as domestic hardship
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum absurdity. Seth's self-pity reaching 'single mother' territory is an absurd leap that's entirely consistent with his victimhood complex. Good economy.

jokes.text: Seth meta-roasts his own class: 'We all know Home Ec is a joke, no offense... Everyone takes this class to get an A. It's bullshit, and I'm sorry.' — said directly to the teacher
jokes.setup: Seth is pleading his case to Mrs. Hayworth
jokes.punchline: He tells the teacher her class is a known joke that students take as a GPA boost — to her face, with repeated apologies
jokes.explanation: Seth's oblivious honesty — insulting the teacher while expecting her sympathy — is a great character note. The repeated 'no offense' and 'I'm sorry' don't mitigate the insults at all, which is the joke. Very Seth.

jokes.text: We all know Home Ec is a joke, no offense. Everyone takes this class to get an A. It's bullshit, and I'm sorry. I'm not putting down your profession, but it's just the way I feel.
jokes.setup: Seth is making his case to Mrs. Hayworth, the Home Ec teacher.
jokes.punchline: He tells the teacher to her face that her class is a joke everyone takes to get an easy A — softening each blow with 'no offense,' 'I'm sorry,' and 'I'm not putting down your profession' in a way that makes it worse.
jokes.explanation: The serial hedges ('no offense / I'm sorry / not putting down your profession') while saying maximally offensive things directly to the teacher's face is a classic cringe-comedy structure. Seth's total sincerity and lack of self-awareness makes it land hard. High character integration — this is specifically Seth's social obliviousness.

jokes.text: Seth and Jules cover a ruined dessert with chocolate — 'The whole thing? Just dump it on. I'm serious.' / 'Now it looks professional.'
jokes.setup: Something has gone wrong with their Home Ec dessert
jokes.punchline: Seth's solution is to dump chocolate over the entire thing — which, somehow, makes it look better

jokes.text: Seth elbows Miroki out of his own conversation: 'Hey, Miroki, could we have a minute alone? Just... Thanks.' Then immediately yells to Evan: 'Dude, Jules is having a fucking party!'

jokes.explanation: The self-defeating request for privacy works well — the joke is in the gap between Seth's attempt at discretion and his complete inability to execute it. 'Just... Thanks.' is a good dismissal beat.

The telling detail that he 'told her what time it was' is Fogell's entire romantic life in four words.

jokes.text: Seth's buildup to the revelation: 'Fine, Evan. Here it comes. When I was a little kid, I kind of had this problem. And it's not even that big of a deal. Something like 8 percent of kids do it...'
jokes.setup: Seth is about to confess why he hates Becca, with ominous build
jokes.punchline: The '8 percent of kids do it' statistic sounds like it's leading to bedwetting or thumb-sucking — the actual confession will be far more absurd
jokes.explanation: Expert misdirection setup. The pseudo-clinical framing ('8 percent of kids') and self-minimizing ('not even that big a deal') work beautifully to lower expectations before the revelation. The setup here is as good as the punchline that follows.

jokes.text: '...and draw pictures of dicks.'
jokes.setup: Seth's lengthy clinical buildup promised a mundane childhood problem
jokes.punchline: He drew pictures of dicks. Compulsively. For hours.
jokes.explanation: One of the best comedic reveals in the film. The punchline is four words delivered after a lengthy misdirection setup. The gap between expectation (bedwetting, thumb-sucking) and reality (compulsive dick illustration) is enormous. The deadpan simplicity of 'and draw pictures of dicks' — after all that buildup — is perfect comedic economy. The pause before the reveal sells it completely. This is a craft-level punchline: original, structurally impeccable, maximally economical, completely earned by the setup.

jokes.text: Evan's stunned clarifications: 'What? Draw pictures of dicks? Dicks? Like a man dick?'
jokes.setup: Seth has just revealed he used to draw pictures of dicks
jokes.punchline: Evan's confirmation process — asking multiple times, refining the category — adds comedic texture to his genuine disbelief
jokes.explanation: The escalation of specificity is excellent: 'What?' → 'Draw pictures of dicks?' → 'Dicks?' → 'Like a man dick?' Each question is funnier than the last because it implies Evan is considering whether there might be a less alarming category of dick. 'Like a man dick?' is a genuinely funny line.

jokes.text: Seth: 'Yeah. Like a man dick. I'd sit there for hours, drawing dicks. I don't know what it was. I couldn't touch the pen to paper without drawing the shape of a penis.'
jokes.setup: Evan is trying to process the revelation
jokes.punchline: Seth's matter-of-fact narration of his compulsion — 'I couldn't touch the pen to paper without drawing the shape of a penis' — delivered with the tone of someone describing a rare neurological condition
jokes.explanation: The clinical self-diagnosis ('I couldn't touch the pen to paper without drawing the shape of a penis') is funny as a heightened way of describing what is objectively just juvenile doodling. The tone is confessional-therapeutic rather than embarrassed.

jokes.text: Seth describes 'the dick operation I had going on' — hiding drawings in a 'Ghostbusters lunchbox'
jokes.setup: Seth is explaining how he concealed his drawings at school
jokes.punchline: He had a full covert operation centered on a Ghostbusters lunchbox — the specificity of the brand is funny, and 'operation' frames the doodling as professional-grade intelligence work
jokes.explanation: The 'Ghostbusters lunchbox' is a perfect period detail that makes the childhood scene vivid. 'Operation' applied to elementary school dick-drawing elevates it nicely. The specificity is what makes it land.

jokes.text: 'So one day I'm finishing up this real big, veiny, triumphant bastard.'
jokes.setup: Seth is describing the day everything went wrong
jokes.punchline: 'A real big, veiny, triumphant bastard' — the pride and craft-specificity applied to a penis drawing, as if discussing a completed masterwork
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the reel. 'Veiny, triumphant bastard' as a description of a child's dick drawing is genuinely inspired — the adjectives carry both aesthetic pride ('triumphant') and anatomical specificity ('veiny'). It frames the drawing as an artistic achievement. The word 'bastard' as an affectionate descriptor for a penis is a perfect finishing touch. Concise, original, maximally funny, deeply character-specific — Seth narrating his childhood drawings like a craftsman describing a finished piece is exactly right.

jokes.text: Evan: 'You hit Becca's foot with your dick?' / Seth: 'Yeah. I know.'
jokes.setup: Seth was finishing a large drawing when something went wrong — there's an offscreen 'Pussy!' shout
jokes.punchline: Evan's summary — 'You hit Becca's foot with your dick?' — condenses the incident to its most absurd essential element. Seth's 'Yeah. I know.' accepts full responsibility.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant economy. We haven't been told what actually happened but Evan's summary — deduced or told off-screen — is perfectly absurd. 'You hit Becca's foot with your dick?' condenses the entire incident to one sentence that is simultaneously completely clear and completely insane. The 18-second gap [17:01 to 17:20] suggests a visual reaction beat or the audience processing the information. Seth's monosyllabic 'Yeah. I know.' is the ideal response — no defense, just resignation.

jokes.text: Becca crying and 'flipping out' leads to the principal finding the 'Ghostbusters lunchbox dick treasure chest'
jokes.setup: Becca has ratted Seth out to the principal
jokes.punchline: 'Ghostbusters lunchbox dick treasure chest' — this naming of the evidence container is both a callback and a fresh comedic escalation
jokes.explanation: 'Ghostbusters lunchbox dick treasure chest' is a great compound noun that makes the lunchbox callback even funnier. The 'treasure chest' framing implies Seth viewed his collection as something precious, which adds a strange dignity to the whole enterprise.

jokes.text: The principal is 'some religious fanatic' who thinks Seth is 'possessed by some dick devil'
jokes.setup: The principal discovers the lunchbox full of dick drawings
jokes.punchline: His interpretation is theological — Seth is possessed by a 'dick devil' — an extreme overreaction that is also internally consistent with fundamentalist thinking
jokes.explanation: 'Dick devil' as a theological concept is an inspired absurdist escalation. The specificity of the principal's interpretation (not just 'troubled kid' but 'possessed by a dick devil') takes the story into wonderful territory.

jokes.text: Seth's parents make him see a therapist 'asking him dick questions' and they 'made him stop eating foods shaped like dicks — no hot dogs, no Popsicles. You know how many foods are shaped like dicks? The best kinds.'
jokes.setup: Seth's parents overreact to the lunchbox discovery
jokes.punchline: The therapeutic intervention expands to dietary restrictions on phallic foods, with Seth's coda: 'You know how many foods are shaped like dicks? The best kinds.'
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The escalation from therapy to dietary restriction is absurdist but grounded — the kind of overcorrection religious families make. 'You know how many foods are shaped like dicks? The best kinds.' is a perfect capping observation — it's both funny as an absurdist non-sequitur AND carries a weird melancholy about Seth being banned from his favorite foods. The casualness of the delivery ('the best kinds') is pitch-perfect Seth. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Evan: 'Super gay.' — after Seth finishes the entire dick-drawing story
jokes.setup: Seth has just delivered a lengthy, detailed account of his childhood dick-drawing compulsion
jokes.punchline: Evan's summary verdict is two words
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy, minimum effort. It lands as a breather laugh after a dense comedic sequence. The simplicity is intentional — a topper that refuses to compete with what just came before.

jokes.text: Seth: 'So I gotta sit and eat dessert alone, like I'm fucking Steven Glanzberg?'
jokes.setup: Seth has to leave for his counselor; Evan can't join him for dessert
jokes.punchline: He invokes 'Steven Glanzberg' — an apparently notorious lone eater — as the worst possible fate
jokes.explanation: The hyper-specific proper noun — 'Steven Glanzberg' as a shorthand for lonely cafeteria loser — is a great comedic technique. It implies a whole social ecosystem that the audience never sees. The specificity makes it funnier than any generic reference would be.

jokes.text: Well, Jules, the funny thing about my back...is that it's located on my cock.
jokes.setup: Jules says 'you scratch our backs, we'll scratch yours' — a standard idiom of reciprocity
jokes.punchline: Seth literalizes 'back' and re-routes it to his genitals, revealing his one-track mind
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect economy joke. The setup is handed to Seth by Jules with an innocent idiom; his response is instantly character-specific (only Seth could say this), perfectly structured, and delivered with mock-sophistication ('the funny thing about my back'). The anatomical re-route is unexpected without being random. It earns its raunch because it simultaneously embarrasses Seth in front of his crush while he's completely oblivious. High quotability; this line is remembered by everyone who's seen the film.

jokes.text: So should I just get a shitload of different shit?
jokes.setup: Jules has been sweetly offering to spend her parents' food money on the party
jokes.punchline: After all the wholesome generosity framing, her casual vulgarity ('shitload of different shit') lands as an absurd tonal pivot
jokes.explanation: A mild laugh from the contrast between Jules' generosity and her blunt phrasing. Functional but not exceptional — the double 'shit' is a small bit of wordplay but it's largely situational.

jokes.text: Kyle's Killer Lemonade. That's kind of gay, but I can get it for you.
jokes.setup: Jules asks Seth to get a specific, cutesy-named alcoholic drink
jokes.punchline: Seth editorializes the brand name as 'kind of gay' while earnestly agreeing to fetch it, revealing his desperate desire to please her despite his reflexive dude-bro judgment
jokes.explanation: Good character work — Seth can't help himself from performing masculine judgment even while completely caving. The contradiction is funny and specific to him. The language is dated/offensive but the joke's comedic engine is solid.

jokes.text: She wants to fuck me. She wants my dick in or around her mouth.
jokes.setup: Seth is trying to convince Evan that Jules asking him to buy alcohol is a romantic overture
jokes.punchline: His logic escalates from 'she thought of me' to immediate graphic sexual conclusion, compressed into two sentences with the comedically specific 'in or around'
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'in or around her mouth' is the comedic gem here — the lawyerly qualifier 'or around' is both absurd and character-perfect for a teenage boy trying to sound casually experienced while revealing total inexperience. The escalation from benign premise to graphic conclusion in two sentences is excellent economy. This line is frequently quoted.

jokes.text: She looked me in the eyes and said: 'Seth, Mom is making a pubie salad. I need some Seth's Own dressing.'
jokes.setup: Evan is rightly skeptical that Jules is using Seth just to get booze; Seth insists she's romantically interested
jokes.punchline: Seth invents a grotesque, nonsensical hypothetical quote to prove his point, referencing 'pubie salad' and a salad dressing named after himself
jokes.explanation: Genuinely original absurdism that doubles as character work. Seth constructs an argument so deranged it proves Evan's point for him. The brand-name construction ('Seth's Own' riffing on Paul Newman's 'Newman's Own') shows real comedic craft. 'Pubie salad' is disgusting in a way that's specific and funny rather than random. The escalating illogic of Seth's reasoning is a running character joke elevated here.

jokes.text: She's D.T.F. She's down to fuck, man. P in vagi.
jokes.setup: Seth has been building his elaborate case for Jules' attraction
jokes.punchline: He punctuates it with a clinical, acronym-then-translation-then-anatomical-abbreviation triple that reduces everything to absurd teenage argot
jokes.explanation: 'P in vagi' as a clinical abbreviation lands as a comedic beat — it's Seth reducing romance to the most transactional possible terms while believing he's being suave. The triple-escalating restatement structure is good; each version is both more explicit and more absurd.

jokes.text: By the time college rolls around, I'll be like the Iron Chef of pounding vag.
jokes.setup: Seth is laying out his two-month romantic roadmap from handjob to girlfriend to college
jokes.punchline: The prestigious culinary metaphor 'Iron Chef' applied to sexual activity, combined with the crude 'pounding vag,' creates maximum incongruity
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in this reel. The joke has multiple layers: the elaborate sexual roadmap is itself funny, then 'Iron Chef' elevates it with an absurd prestige metaphor, then 'of pounding vag' drops it back into crude teenage reality. It's a masterclass in register collision. The specificity of the TV show reference (not just 'chef' but 'Iron Chef') shows real comedic craftsmanship. Extremely quotable — this line has had genuine cultural longevity from the film. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in quality and arguably exceeds it in impact.

jokes.text: Hey, Greg, why don't you go piss your pants again? / That was eight years ago, asshole. / People don't forget.
jokes.setup: Seth wants to get Greg off his case; he digs up a childhood embarrassment
jokes.punchline: Greg's defensive 'that was eight years ago' is immediately destroyed by Seth's deadpan 'people don't forget'
jokes.explanation: The three-beat structure is tight and professional. The power is in the economy of the final line — 'People don't forget' is four words that land with devastating finality. It doubles as absurdist wisdom (this is not sage advice, it's weaponized) and perfect Seth character work. The setup-defense-counterpunch structure is classic comedy construction executed cleanly.

jokes.text: We could be that mistake!
jokes.setup: Seth is pitching Evan on the plan to get girls drunk so they hook up. He frames it with the relatable female experience of regretting drunken sex.
jokes.punchline: Instead of showing any self-awareness about how predatory this framing is, Seth enthusiastically positions them as the desired outcome ('that mistake')
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly compressed. The joke works on multiple levels: Seth's obliviousness to the self-deprecating nature of positioning yourself as 'the mistake'; the dark subversion of rom-com wish-fulfillment; and the genuine enthusiasm of the delivery. The exclamation point in his delivery of something most people would be ashamed to say is the core of the gag. This is a quotable line that also reveals character depth (or lack thereof) efficiently.

jokes.text: Where's that sack of shit, Fogell? He said he'd be here. I'm here with my thumb up my ass.
jokes.setup: Seth and Evan are waiting for Fogell, who is late
jokes.punchline: The standard complaint about waiting is punched up with 'thumb up my ass' as the idiomatic expression of his impatience
jokes.explanation: Functional Seth-voice complaint. The idiom is colorful but not especially inventive. It's the kind of line that gets a small laugh from Seth's relentless vulgarity but doesn't have the structural craft of his better moments.

jokes.text: Wait, you changed your name to McLovin?
jokes.setup: Fogell has finally arrived with his fake ID; Seth and Evan expectantly check it
jokes.punchline: The name on the ID is revealed to be 'McLovin' — a single absurd surname, no first name
jokes.explanation: The reveal of 'McLovin' is one of the great comedic moments in 2000s film. The name itself is the joke — it's not a real name, it doesn't sound like a real name, it's simultaneously Irish-sounding and a portmanteau of 'Mac' + 'lovin' suggesting sexual appetite. The simplicity of the reaction ('you changed your name to McLovin?') perfectly mirrors audience response. The choice of a single-name ID with no first name adds a second layer. This moment launched a genuine cultural phenomenon — 'McLovin' became a widely-known reference. High marks across the board for a premise joke.

jokes.text: McLovin? What kind of a stupid name is that? Are you an Irish R&B singer?
jokes.setup: Seth has just absorbed the shock of 'McLovin'
jokes.punchline: He invents the specific absurd niche of 'Irish R&B singer' as the only possible context where this name makes sense
jokes.explanation: The 'Irish R&B singer' line is a great follow-up to the McLovin reveal. The specificity of the cultural intersection (Irish + R&B) is unexpected and funny, and it nails the actual quality of the name — it does sound like a stage name in an improbable genre. Seth's ability to generate absurd cultural comparisons in real time is a character trait this joke exemplifies well.

jokes.text: It was between that or Mohammad. / Why the fuck would it be between that or Mohammad? / Mohammad is the most common name on earth. Read a fucking book.
jokes.setup: Seth demands to know why Fogell picked 'McLovin' when he could have used a normal name
jokes.punchline: Fogell's explanation that his only other option was 'Mohammad' makes no logical sense; Seth's correction that Mohammad is the world's most common name both validates and deepens the absurdity
jokes.explanation: The three-beat exchange works because Seth's outrage is completely reasonable (why just those two options?) and the 'Read a fucking book' closer punches with Seth's particular brand of exasperated authority. Fogell's inexplicable logic is a perfect character beat — he's not dumb, he's just operating on an alien wavelength.

jokes.text: Have you ever met anyone named Mohammad? / Have you ever met anyone named McLovin? / No, that's why you picked a dumb fucking name.
jokes.setup: Seth argues McLovin is an unusual name
jokes.punchline: Fogell uses Seth's own logic against him — the rarity of the name should make it more believable, not less — and Seth can only respond with circular insistence
jokes.explanation: Fogell actually wins this logical exchange, which is funny because Seth was right that the name is terrible but wrong in his reasoning. The ping-pong structure ('Have you ever met anyone named X?') is clean and well-executed. Seth's inability to counter the argument and retreating to blunt assertion ('dumb fucking name') is perfect.

jokes.text: You look like a future pedophile in this picture, number one. Number two, it doesn't even have a first name. It just says McLovin! One name? Who are you, Seal?
jokes.setup: Seth is cataloguing everything wrong with Fogell's fake ID

jokes.explanation: The structured complaint list is satisfying comedy architecture. 'Future pedophile' is harsh but landed via Seth's mock-forensic delivery. The 'Who are you, Seal?' comparison is excellent — Seal is specifically chosen because he's internationally famous but known by one name, which parallels what Fogell has apparently aspired to. The reference is current-era-specific without feeling dated. Strong multi-part joke.

jokes.text: Every day, hundreds of kids go into the liquor store with fake IDs, and every single one says they're 21. How many 21-year-olds are in this town? It's called fucking strategy.
jokes.setup: Seth criticizes that Fogell made the ID say he's 25 instead of 21
jokes.punchline: Fogell's rebuttal is delivered with supreme confidence but its logic only partially holds — it's the reasoning of someone who is both smarter and dumber than Seth at the same time
jokes.explanation: Fogell's character is defined by this joke — he's the person who over-engineers a problem that required basic execution. The 'fucking strategy' button on a genuinely somewhat-reasonable argument makes the whole thing funnier: he's not entirely wrong, but he's completely wrong in context. Good character-comedy work.

jokes.text: I am McLovin.
jokes.setup: Seth is ranting about how 'McLovin' is a ridiculous name that has never existed
jokes.punchline: Fogell's simple, serene declaration — 'I am McLovin' — delivered as a moment of personal identity affirmation
jokes.explanation: Three words. This is the comedic economy scoring a 10 — maximum joke per word. The setup is Seth's extended rant about how no one is McLovin and McLovin doesn't exist. Fogell's calm, zen response transforms a fake ID gag into an unexpected character moment of self-actualization. It's funny, weirdly touching, and perfectly delivered. The joke works because it subverts expectation completely — we expect pushback or capitulation, not identity commitment. Among the most quotable lines in the film.

jokes.setup: Fogell has just serenely declared 'I am McLovin'

jokes.explanation: Seth's reaction to Fogell's calm is the counter-joke. The 'fairy-tale name' phrase is a funny specific word choice for an argument about a fake ID. His rant ending on the blunt 'you fuck' is a Seth character staple. Solid but overshadowed by the Fogell response it's answering.

jokes.text: Man, don't you have any non-infant clothes?
jokes.setup: Seth has gone to Evan's house to change clothes before the party
jokes.punchline: Seth's critique of Evan's wardrobe as 'non-infant clothes' implies everything Evan owns is sized/styled for a baby

jokes.text: No one's gotten a handjob in cargo shorts since Nam.

jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the film and the standout joke of this reel. Structurally perfect: the setup is mundane (why change clothes?), the punchline collapses sexual anxiety, fashion criticism, and Vietnam War history into a single sentence. 'Since Nam' is the key — it's an absurd historical anchor that implies a continuous tradition of handjob-cargo-short incompatibility dating back to 1968. The joke is completely original, maximally economic, and purely Seth. This is the kind of line that becomes a cultural quote across demographics. Comparable to the 9.5/10 anchor examples in quality.

jokes.text: These fucking terrorists multiply like bunnies. Where did I leave the M16?
jokes.setup: Seth is frustrated that his plan to change clothes has been complicated (his car was towed, his parents might see)
jokes.punchline: He extends a military metaphor to his mundane clothing problem, complete with asking for an M16
jokes.explanation: The military metaphor for teenage inconveniences is a Seth-voice joke but it's not particularly sharp here. The M16 reference extends the bit but doesn't elevate it. Functional filler comedy.

jokes.text: Do you have any bigger clothes or do you only shop at babyGap?
jokes.setup: Seth is rummaging through Evan's clothes looking for something to wear
jokes.punchline: 'babyGap' as the specific brand — not just 'baby clothes' but the actual retail chain for infants — is funnier than a generic insult
jokes.explanation: Callback to the infant-clothes gag that lands better with the brand specificity. 'babyGap' is a real store with cultural recognition, making the insult more precise. The callback structure gives it a slight bonus but it's still a relatively mild joke.

jokes.text: It's a fucking vest, dumbass. / You look like Pinocchio.
jokes.setup: Fogell has found a vest in what appears to be Evan's father's wardrobe and is wearing it to 'look older'
jokes.punchline: Evan's 'You look like Pinocchio' — the puppet, not an adult — perfectly undercuts Fogell's goal
jokes.explanation: The Pinocchio comparison is well-chosen: Pinocchio is associated with childhood, with puppethood, and (bonus) with lying — all relevant to Fogell's situation. It's a quick, economical visual insult that lands. Good but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Now Seth's gonna pick up all the pieces.
jokes.setup: Seth has just delivered an ultimatum to Fogell about stealing alcohol from his workplace
jokes.punchline: Seth narrates his own heroism in the third person with the grandiosity of a movie protagonist
jokes.explanation: Third-person self-aggrandizement is a classic Seth-character beat. Funny because he's deeply unqualified for the heroic framing he's applying to buying party alcohol. Good character voice, not exceptional construction.

jokes.text: You still haven't told him that we're rooming together? / Fogell, shut the fuck up.
jokes.setup: Evan and Fogell are hiding from Seth in a room, whispering; Fogell innocently raises the fact that Evan and Fogell are rooming together at college — information Seth hasn't been told
jokes.punchline: The revelation that there's a secret Seth doesn't know, dropped at the worst possible moment, with Evan's panicked 'shut the fuck up' as instant damage control
jokes.explanation: Important plot-comedy beat that plants the Seth/Evan friendship tension. The timing (mid-crisis, whispering, Seth potentially nearby) adds to the comedy. This gets a rewatch bonus because viewers re-appreciate the moment knowing how the roommate storyline develops. The cringe of Fogell innocently dropping the bomb is well-deployed.

jokes.text: Hope piggy can run. [Seth attempting to steal from the liquor store]
jokes.setup: Seth has declared he's going to steal the alcohol from the store where Fogell's boss works
jokes.punchline: His self-motivating war cry — 'Hope piggy can run' — is both a threat to himself and an admission that his plan is to run, implying he knows this will go wrong
jokes.explanation: Self-aware self-deprecation ('piggy') deployed as bravado is an interesting combination. The line is punchy and confident while actually containing the seeds of failure. Rewatch bonus: knowing he fails makes this funnier in retrospect.

jokes.text: Twenty-two. / You certainly are. That'll be 80 dollars.
jokes.setup: Seth tries to charm an older woman at a store (seemingly non-liquor store), possibly attempting to get her to buy alcohol
jokes.punchline: The woman's 'you certainly are' is ambiguous — it confirms his age claim ('twenty-two') with no apparent suspicion, suggesting she either believes him or doesn't care
jokes.explanation: A quick transactional comedy beat. The deadpan acceptance is mild humor. The '80 dollars' grounding it in reality is a small additional beat.

jokes.text: Would you like me to buy you alcohol? / That would be lovely. / Enjoy your remaining years. / I will. / Enjoy fucking Jules. / I will.
jokes.setup: Seth helps an elderly woman pick up her dropped purse
jokes.punchline: The parallel structure — where 'enjoy your remaining years' and 'enjoy fucking Jules' are treated with identical casual warmth by both parties — creates an absurdist exchange; the elderly woman seems perfectly fine wishing him luck with 'fucking Jules'
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant. The parallel construction of the exchange is what makes it work: both parties give each other genuine, caring send-offs — one about mortality, one about sex with a teenager — and both respond with equal warmth. 'Enjoy your remaining years' is itself a darkly funny thing to say to an elderly stranger. The elderly woman's unfazed 'I will' to 'enjoy fucking Jules' is the perfect button. This is tight comedic writing with a dark edge.

jokes.text: Don't do it, kid. [Seth hesitates at the liquor store door] / I never had a choice. [Seth walks in]

jokes.punchline: The hardboiled noir framing ('I never had a choice') applied to a teenage boy stealing booze for a party is maximum-incongruity comedy
jokes.explanation: The genre parody here is effective — Seth styling himself as a noir protagonist heading into a dangerous heist, when the stakes are mild teenage mischief. 'I never had a choice' is a great noir cliché delivered completely straight. The two-part structure (warning/response) is clean.

jokes.text: You fucking killed her! / No!
jokes.setup: Seth has gone into the liquor store to steal; something goes catastrophically wrong
jokes.punchline: The accusation 'You fucking killed her!' after what appears to be Seth colliding with/knocking over someone (presumably the elderly woman or another customer) is the explosion of the already-established tension
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy payoff. The abruptness and extremity of 'you fucking killed her' in response to what is surely an accidental stumble/knock is funny through sheer escalation. The 'No!' response suggests Seth's complete denial/panic. Gets rewatch bonus as the setup for a later callback.

jokes.text: Where's all the stolen liquor? Did you hide it up your butt?
jokes.setup: Fogell returns without the stolen liquor after Seth presumably failed spectacularly
jokes.punchline: Seth demands the stolen liquor and suggests the only place it could be is hidden in Fogell's body
jokes.explanation: Classic Seth verbal aggression — the butt-hiding question is both accusatory and absurd. Decent but not extraordinary; it's one of several similar Seth lines in the reel.

jokes.text: We're gonna get alcohol for the whole party, okay? We put a lot of time into this list, so don't fuck it up. It's perfect.
jokes.setup: Seth hands Fogell a list and money to buy alcohol, delivering it with extreme gravity
jokes.punchline: The gap between the import Seth places on the list ('a lot of time,' 'it's perfect') and the reality that it's a list of party booze is classic Seth self-importance comedy
jokes.explanation: Seth's operational self-importance over minor tasks is a consistent character bit. Here it's functional — the list includes things like 'ouzo' and 'Kyle's Killer Lemonade' which undermines the military briefing tone. Decent but familiar from earlier in the film.

jokes.text: Goldslick Vodka. That's for Becca. Don't forget that.
jokes.setup: Seth is reading through the booze list; Goldslick Vodka was established as Becca's specific request
jokes.punchline: The solemnity with which Seth protects Becca's specific vodka order — as if it were sacred cargo — is funny given his earlier explicit planning for getting her drunk
jokes.explanation: Mild callback that works because we know the full context of why Seth is so protective of Becca's order. Character-consistent without being especially funny on its own.

jokes.text: I should have wore the vest.
jokes.setup: Fogell is paralyzed with nerves outside the liquor store
jokes.punchline: He regrets not wearing the vest — his 'disguise' that everyone mocked — as if it were actual protective armor

jokes.text: Then I'll cut your dumb fucking face off...throw it over mine and get your ID and buy it my fucking self!
jokes.setup: Seth threatens Fogell if he doesn't go in; Fogell points out logically that killing him won't get Seth the alcohol since Fogell has the ID
jokes.punchline: Seth's alternative plan — facial transplant to access the ID — is a spectacular escalation of absurd problem-solving that only Seth would arrive at
jokes.explanation: Genuinely excellent escalation. Seth's logic chain — murder doesn't work because ID won't work without Fogell's face, therefore face transplant — is both insane and internally consistent, which is the hallmark of great absurdist comedy. The specificity ('throw it over mine') elevates it beyond generic movie-threat to something with real comedic craft. Character-perfect: Seth would absolutely arrive at this conclusion.

jokes.text: Oh, really? You don't have the technology or the steady hands to pull off a procedure like that, so ha!
jokes.setup: Seth has just threatened to perform a facial transplant on Fogell
jokes.punchline: Fogell's rebuttal focuses entirely on Seth's lack of SURGICAL CAPABILITY rather than on the moral/legal problem of murder — suggesting this is a valid concern if Seth had better hands
jokes.explanation: The best counter-joke in the reel. Fogell's concern is exclusively about Seth's surgical competence, not the ethics or the murder. This reveals Fogell's precise, analytical character — he argues the most specific objection possible. 'So ha!' as a triumphant button on a facial-transplant argument is an unexpected touch of nerdish victory. The exchange as a whole (Jokes 35+36) is the best two-line back-and-forth in the reel.

jokes.text: Oh, really? You don't have the technology or the steady hands to pull off a procedure like that, so ha!
jokes.setup: Seth threatens to cut off Fogell's face for the ID
jokes.punchline: Fogell's rebuttal is not 'that's insane' or 'you'd go to prison' — it's a calm, clinical assessment of Seth's surgical incompetence, ending with a triumphant 'ha!'
jokes.explanation: The joke is in what Fogell does NOT say. He doesn't object on moral or legal grounds — he objects purely on procedural grounds ('you don't have the technology or the steady hands'). This is perfect Fogell character work: clinical, nerd-authoritative, and completely missing the point of why face-removal is bad. The 'ha!' is a wonderful button — schoolyard triumphalism from a boy who just accepted that face transplants are on the table.

jokes.text: Sir, did you do this? On the floor? / No. / And you should really clean this up. Someone could really hurt themselves. / Fuck my life.
jokes.setup: In the liquor store, Seth is apparently responsible for something on the floor (dropped/broken bottles, possibly from an earlier mishap)
jokes.punchline: He denies responsibility, is then lectured about safety, and punctuates his entire humiliation with 'Fuck my life' — a perfect character response to cascading failure
jokes.explanation: Good cringe beat. The 'someone could really hurt themselves' passive safety lecture to someone who just caused the mess, followed by Seth's completely defeated 'Fuck my life,' is a solid humiliation escalation. The deadpan delivery of the safety warning is the key element.

jokes.text: Hey, so did you bring a condom for tonight? / I brought a little bottle of spermicidal lube too.
jokes.setup: In the middle of their liquor crisis, Evan casually asks about condoms
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'condom' to 'also spermicidal lube' reveals that Evan has prepared a full prophylactic kit for a hookup that isn't guaranteed to happen
jokes.explanation: Good character-differentiating moment. Evan's over-preparation (lube for a maybe-hookup) versus Seth's zero-preparation is a character contrast that lands. The timing (brought up mid-crisis) is part of the joke. 'Spermicidal lube' is funny partly from the clinical term, partly from the absurd forward-planning it implies.

jokes.text: I was gonna go down on her for, like, several hours, okay? She would love that. She'd be smitten. She'd go out with that. Or I dry hump the shit out of her leg.
jokes.setup: Evan criticizes Seth for not bringing a condom; Seth defends that he had his own plan
jokes.punchline: Seth's 'plan' escalates from 'several hours of oral sex' (grandiose ambition) to 'dry hump her leg' (complete capitulation) in two sentences — the fall from romantic to desperate is the entire joke
jokes.explanation: The arc from 'several hours' of oral sex (which is itself grandiose teenager fantasy) to the retreat position of 'dry hump the shit out of her leg' is a beautifully constructed deflation. The confidence of 'she'd be smitten' giving way to canine-level intimacy is pure Seth-character comedy. 'Several hours' is the key modifier — not just oral sex, but heroic quantities of it.

jokes.text: 'Oh, Evan. Thank you for bringing that lube for my pussy. I never would've been able to handle your fucking 4-inch dick inside my pussy without that gigantic bottle of lube.'
jokes.setup: Seth is criticizing Evan for bringing spermicidal lube, calling it 'psycho shit'
jokes.punchline: Seth voices Becca's imagined reaction in a sarcastic impersonation, loading it with both a penis-size insult directed at Evan and an absurd complaint about the bottle size
jokes.explanation: The impersonation is funny because Seth commits to the voice, includes a gratuitous personal insult ('4-inch'), and the specificity of 'gigantic bottle' implies Evan brought something comically oversized. The joke slightly overstays with the repeated 'pussy' but the insult-within-sarcasm structure works.

jokes.text: These girls are 18, they're not dried-up old ladies. They're good to go.
jokes.setup: Seth's final argument against lube
jokes.punchline: The clinical sexual authority of 'they're good to go' as the conclusion of a lube-necessity debate, as if Seth has medical expertise
jokes.explanation: Modest laugh. Seth's authoritative sexual pronouncements are a recurring bit; this one is weaker because it's a dismissal rather than an escalation. 'Good to go' is the funniest phrase but the setup is weak.

jokes.text: Oh, shit, it's Cary Hutchins. / She had the biggest tits I've ever seen. / I heard she got breast-reduction surgery. / What? Making your tits smaller? That's like slapping God for giving you a gorgeous gift.
jokes.setup: In the middle of the liquor store crisis, Seth spots a woman he recognizes
jokes.punchline: The breast-reduction news leads Seth to respond with religious indignation — 'slapping God for giving you a gorgeous gift' — as if breast reduction is theological blasphemy
jokes.explanation: The 'slapping God' construction is strong — it takes a typical teenage boy sentiment (objecting to breast reduction) and elevates it to cosmic moral outrage. The religious framing is absurd and specific; Seth is not religious elsewhere, making this purely performative theology in service of ogling. Good character work and a quotable, well-constructed line.

jokes.text: She had back problems, man. And it's not just making them smaller. They completely reshape them. They make them more supple and symmetrical. / I gotta catch a glimpse of these warlocks. / Let's make a move.
jokes.setup: Evan defends Cary's surgery on medical and aesthetic grounds
jokes.punchline: Seth processes Evan's description of the reshaping surgery and concludes he must see the results, calling them 'warlocks' — an absurd term for breasts that implies dark mystical power
jokes.explanation: 'Warlocks' is the kind of absurd teenage slang that feels both invented-in-the-moment and immediately intuitive. The word choice suggests mythical, dangerous power — which is funny in the context of a boy being drawn to a woman in a liquor store against his better judgment. 'Let's make a move' as a tactical declaration about ogling is a good button.

jokes.text: I don't believe it! [repeated multiple times as Seth discovers his stolen liquor is gone]
jokes.setup: Seth has been trying to conceal stolen liquor and something has gone catastrophically wrong with that plan
jokes.punchline: The repeated 'I don't believe it' — escalating with each repetition — becomes funnier through sheer exasperated repetition and total disbelief
jokes.explanation: Escalating reaction beats are a low-craft comedy staple but Seth's complete disbelief delivers. The repetition is functional; it's not clever writing but it's effective performance-driven comedy.

jokes.text: I don't know, man. I think she looked better before. But now that she can jog comfortably, she's in the best shape she's ever...
jokes.setup: Seth and Evan have been chasing Cary Hutchins to see the results of her surgery; Evan is delivering his verdict
jokes.punchline: Evan's conclusion pivots from aesthetic disappointment to a clinical commendation of her jogging ability — the mid-crisis fitness evaluation is absurdist deadpan
jokes.explanation: The callback to Evan's earlier defense ('back problems, now she can jog') works beautifully as a punctuation on the entire bit. Evan has absorbed the medical justification so thoroughly that he applies it in his aesthetic review. The trailing off mid-crisis ('...she's in the best shape she's ever—') is a perfect structural choice.

jokes.text: Holy shit, they busted Fogell.
jokes.setup: Through the store window, Seth sees Fogell being stopped by police
jokes.punchline: The simultaneous spectacle of Seth's own disaster inside the store and Fogell's arrest outside — both happening at once — is the comedic peak of the sequence
jokes.explanation: The situational comedy here is strong even if the line itself isn't — the two disasters converging is well-timed filmmaking. The reaction beat earns its score from the simultaneous chaos rather than the words.

jokes.text: He assaulted the customer, grabbed the cash and ran out. / How...? How...? How...? / Say when, height-wise. / I'm gonna start up here, tell me when.
jokes.setup: Officers are interviewing the store clerk about the crime; a second officer offers to demonstrate height using his own body
jokes.punchline: The detective's physical demonstration method — starting at the top of his body and asking the clerk to say 'when' — is both professionally absurd and visually funny as a height-reference technique
jokes.explanation: The cops are established as comedically incompetent throughout the film; this 'say when, height-wise' methodology is a good bit of detective-parody. Procedural incompetence comedy done with light touch.

jokes.text: Was he African? / African... / No. He was American, and he was like you. He looked just like you. / He was Jewish. Okay, Jew. / It's an odd crime for a Jew. / They're pretty docile.
jokes.setup: The officers are trying to identify the suspect's ethnicity through the worst possible process
jokes.punchline: The clerk identifies the suspect as 'Jewish' and the officer's response — 'it's an odd crime for a Jew' — followed by 'they're pretty docile' — is absurdist ethnic-stereotype-as-police-work comedy that indicts the officers as obliviously prejudiced
jokes.explanation: The cops-as-culturally-oblivious-idiots joke works because the stereotyping is applied with the same professional deadpan as actual police work. 'They're pretty docile' as a criminological assessment of Jewish people is so absurd it's clearly satirizing police incompetence rather than endorsing the view. The ethnic confusion escalation ('African? American? Jewish?') is well-constructed.

jokes.text: I have an exam tomorrow! / I have a goddamn veterinary exam! / Well, apparently someone has an exam.
jokes.setup: The store clerk interrupts the police investigation to complain about his upcoming veterinary exam
jokes.punchline: The officer's perfectly deadpan observation 'Well, apparently someone has an exam' — as if this were useful information rather than an irrelevant complaint — is the button
jokes.explanation: Classic straight-man deadpan. 'Well, apparently someone has an exam' takes the clerk's outburst and reformats it as a neutral observation, which is funnier than any combative response would be. The officer's unflappable delivery of non-sequitur commentary is excellent comedic timing. The 'goddamn veterinary exam' specificity also helps — not just any exam, but a vet exam.

jokes.text: It's M... McLov... McLovin. / McLovin? / Now, what's your first name? / My first name? / Technically I don't have a first name, so don't worry about my first name.
jokes.setup: The police are questioning Fogell/McLovin and ask for his name
jokes.punchline: Fogell's stumbling entry into 'McLovin' followed by the revelation that there's no first name — reassured by his 'don't worry about my first name' — is a perfect payoff on the ID joke
jokes.explanation: Brilliant callback structure. The stumble into the name ('M... McLov... McLovin') mirrors the original reveal's shock. 'Don't worry about my first name' is the standout — it's delivered as if the officer's concern is misplaced, as if everyone knows you just don't ask McLovin about his first name. Fogell has fully committed to the persona, which is both funny and oddly heroic. The officer's repetition of 'McLovin?' echoes Seth's original reaction, creating a satisfying structural mirror.

jokes.text: That's badass. / That is badass. / Really cool. / A badass name. / Lot of people with weird names. / Chingy. Shakira. / Rafe. Pax.
jokes.setup: The officers confirm Fogell's single-name ID situation
jokes.punchline: Instead of treating it as suspicious, the cops bond over it and list celebrity single-namers — including oddly specific choices like 'Pax' — revealing their total incompetence as authority figures
jokes.explanation: The cops undermining themselves with celebrity-name bonding is a great character bit. 'Rafe. Pax.' are funnier than the more famous names because they're more obscure — the cops have done real work to come up with these examples, which reveals misplaced priorities. 'That's badass' as a cop's reaction to a teenage fake-ID suspect is perfect establishment of the film's cop-character comedy.

jokes.text: We arrested a man-lady who was legally named 'Fuck.' / Think he was Vietnamese, it was with a P-H. / But it's still shocking to see on a license.
jokes.setup: Officers continue their casual conversation about unusual names
jokes.punchline: The story of arresting someone named 'Fuck' is itself the joke, then 'with a P-H' provides a second-layer of commitment (the name is 'Phuck,' still phonetically 'Fuck'), and 'still shocking to see on a license' is the button
jokes.explanation: Three-beat structure that escalates perfectly. 'We arrested a man-lady named Fuck' is already strong; 'with a P-H' shows the cop has thought carefully about this phonetic technicality; 'still shocking to see on a license' is the perfect deadpan button — acknowledging that the spelling doesn't diminish the visual impact. The 'man-lady' phrase also adds a layer of cop-character voice (casual, oblivious). One of the stronger cop-subplot jokes.

jokes.text: How old are you, McLovin? / Old enough. / Old enough for what? / To party.
jokes.setup: Officer asks McLovin's age; Fogell, emboldened by their apparent approval, deploys the classic non-answer 'old enough'
jokes.punchline: The officer's deadpan follow-up 'old enough for what?' forces Fogell to complete the idiom, which he does with the magnificent anticlimax 'to party'
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-step structure. The first surprise is Fogell having the gall to respond 'old enough' to a police officer who literally just saw his questionable ID. The second is that the officer doesn't let it slide — he applies literal police-questioning logic to the idiom. Fogell's 'to party' is the ideal response: it's the only answer to that question, it's exactly what a teenager would say, and it's delivered with the confidence of McLovin. Highly quotable, great character moment, and the economy is impeccable.

jokes.text: "It's just like a woman. Even after you're dead, they wanna tear your heart out." — Slater's organ-donor wife joke, delivered weekly and still celebrated by both cops.
jokes.setup: Slater reveals he's an organ donor because his wife insisted, framing it as her controlling him.
jokes.punchline: He turns organ donation into a misogynist zinger and proudly admits he repeats it weekly — the meta-celebration of a mediocre joke is part of the joke.
jokes.explanation: The real joke isn't the organ-donor punchline itself — it's middling — but the layer where Slater brags he says it weekly and his partner confirms it still makes him laugh. That self-satisfied mediocrity is a sharp character beat. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: "Why waste 2 bucks? We'll take you. No problem." — Cops volunteer to give the mugging victim a ride to gather information, immediately segueing into shaking him down.
jokes.setup: The cops position themselves as helpful officers offering a kind ride to a victim.
jokes.punchline: Their actual motive is entirely self-serving — getting information and implicitly exploiting the situation — undercutting the Good Samaritan framing.
jokes.explanation: Mild ironic beat — cops performing helpfulness while extracting value. Sets up the corrupt-cop comedy thread but isn't particularly sharp on its own.

jokes.text: "I have a warrant out for a totally nonviolent crime. Okay? There. Mercy Street, guys."
jokes.setup: The mugging victim is begging not to be reported and confessing to the cops to explain his desperation.
jokes.punchline: He preemptively qualifies his criminal record as "totally nonviolent" — as if that earns him sympathy — and the vague "Mercy Street" appeal is pathetically earnest.
jokes.explanation: Nicely economical. The qualifier "totally nonviolent" does a lot of work — it implies he has multiple warrants and knows exactly how to categorize them. "Mercy Street" is a funny, slightly absurd plea. Solid mid-tier joke.

jokes.text: "You better get us a shitload of cash or a shitload of alcohol, or you're going to fucking prison." — Michaels extorting the victim with Slater immediately pumping the brakes.
jokes.setup: The cops are ostensibly taking the victim to get information. Slater has been playing it cool.
jokes.punchline: Michaels abruptly drops the pretense and baldly extorts the guy, while Slater — the ostensibly more corrupt senior cop — tries to walk it back, flipping the expected dynamic.
jokes.explanation: The inversion works well — it's the junior cop who goes full criminal while the senior one plays straight man. "A shitload of cash OR a shitload of alcohol" is funny in its equivalence of those two things. Good character specificity.

jokes.text: "Seven dollars? What the fuck? This isn't enough. What are you, 6 years old?"
jokes.setup: The victim has been shaken down for cash and produces his entire wallet.
jokes.punchline: Seven dollars — the pathetic amount undercuts any tension, and comparing him to a 6-year-old is a perfect contemptuous escalation.
jokes.explanation: "Seven dollars" is a great specific number — not five, not ten. The "6 years old" comparison is contemptuous in an absurdly precise way. Good economy, punches above its weight.

jokes.text: "There's, like, tons of liquor there, all right? And I can definitely get you, like, tons of liquor, like so much liquor, so..." — Fogell/McLovin nervously pitching the party liquor to the cops.
jokes.setup: McLovin is trying to negotiate his way out of a police shakedown by promising alcohol at a party.
jokes.punchline: His pitch dissolves into repetitive filler — "tons of liquor, like so much liquor, so..." — trailing off into nothing, perfectly capturing an anxious teenager bluffing.
jokes.explanation: McLovin's verbal collapse under pressure is pitch-perfect character work. The repetition of "tons of liquor" with diminishing coherence is a great performance beat even on the page. High character integration score because only a nervous, socially inept kid would pitch this badly.

jokes.text: "I don't like this idea. This guy's fucking creepy, man. Look at him." / "What? He looks like a guy. That's what guys look like."
jokes.setup: Seth and Evan are debating whether to trust the random dude McLovin just negotiated with to get them booze.
jokes.punchline: Evan's defense — "he looks like a guy, that's what guys look like" — is hilariously circular and reveals his naivety. It's the most useless reassurance possible.
jokes.explanation: "He looks like a guy. That's what guys look like." is a great line — perfectly economical, deeply stupid logic delivered with sincerity. It's the kind of line that gets quoted. High quotability. Character-specific to Evan's oblivious earnestness.

jokes.text: "You promised Becca you'd get her alcohol. If you don't, she's gonna have a shitty night. That's all I'm saying."
jokes.setup: Seth is trying to convince Evan to follow through with the sketchy alcohol plan.
jokes.punchline: Framing Becca's potential disappointment in alcohol procurement as the moral stakes is both funny in its triviality and reveals Seth's self-serving logic (he wants the alcohol for his own romantic aims).
jokes.explanation: Functional character beat that illustrates Seth's rationalization skills, but it's not a punchy joke so much as comedic dialogue texture.

jokes.text: "Buses smell like piss, generally." / "You know why?" / "People piss on them."
jokes.setup: Slater is persuading McLovin not to take the bus, noting buses smell like piss.
jokes.punchline: McLovin asks why, clearly expecting some sociological insight; Slater's answer is a tautological "people piss on them" — delivered as wisdom.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three lines, circular logic, deadpan delivery. Slater's tautological wisdom (the bus smells like piss because people piss on it) is funny because it's simultaneously correct and useless. The structure is a classic misdirect: you expect an insight, you get a non-answer stated with authority.

jokes.text: "You know, one of you bros could've come up and sat up with me." — McLovin, riding in the cop car, mildly complaining about being abandoned in the front seat.
jokes.setup: McLovin is riding in the front seat of the cop car while the cops chat; there's an implied awkwardness.
jokes.punchline: He calls them "bros" and frames his isolation as a social slight — as if he's bummed his pals didn't want to hang — which is both endearing and absurd given the circumstance.
jokes.explanation: Solid character beat. McLovin calling the cops "bros" and expressing mild social FOMO is funny because of the absurd dynamic — he's essentially bonding with his kidnappers. Character-specific but not exceptional.

jokes.text: "She called, she said, 'I can't wait for you to get there.' That sounds like she fully wants it, man! Oh, yeah! Who's gonna give it to her, huh, my man? You, that's who."
jokes.setup: Seth overhears Evan's phone call with Jules and immediately interprets her friendly excitement as sexual invitation.
jokes.punchline: Seth's breathless sexual overinterpretation of a completely innocuous phone call is the joke — his desperation and projection are both funny and sad.
jokes.explanation: Functional teen-comedy material. Seth's horndog overinterpretation is consistent with his character but the joke isn't particularly crafted — it's just him being loud and horny, which is his baseline.

jokes.text: "You guys on MySpace, or...?" — McLovin awkwardly attempting small talk with the cops.
jokes.setup: An awkward silence in the cop car following the conversation about being dropped off.
jokes.punchline: McLovin attempts to break the ice with the most transparently teen-speak icebreaker possible — asking cops if they're on MySpace — capturing his social ineptitude and the generational gulf perfectly.
jokes.explanation: One of the best McLovin moments in this reel. Three words do enormous work: they establish the generational gap, McLovin's social desperation, and the absurdity of the cop-kid dynamic. Period-perfect (2007 MySpace) and completely character-specific — only McLovin would reach for this. The subsequent silence (implied by the scene beat) amplifies it. Comparable to the '8.0 anchor' in economy and character integration.

jokes.text: "How am I supposed to find one guy? This job really isn't how, you know, shows like CSI make it out to be."
jokes.setup: The victim clarifies it was only one mugger, not multiple. Slater had been prepared to dismiss the case.
jokes.punchline: Slater uses the corrected detail to make the case sound HARDER, not easier, and blames CSI for unrealistic expectations — hilariously inverting logic.
jokes.explanation: Good inverted logic — one guy should be easier, but Slater makes it sound impossible. The CSI reference grounds it culturally and reveals his genuine delusion about policing. Solid mid-tier joke.

jokes.text: "When I first joined the force, I assumed there was semen on everything... and there was some, like, huge semen database that had every bad guy's semen in it. There isn't."
jokes.setup: Slater is lamenting how policing doesn't match TV expectations (CSI).
jokes.punchline: He fixates specifically on semen — conjuring a detailed fantasy about a vast semen database — delivered with genuine nostalgic disappointment.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in this reel. The specificity of 'huge semen database with every bad guy's semen in it' is brilliantly absurd — the more he elaborates, the funnier it gets. Slater's genuine disappointment ('there isn't') is the perfect deadpan kicker. Highly quotable and original. The phrase 'semen on everything' captures exactly how a dumb cop would process CSI. Approaches the 8.0 anchor in quality.

jokes.text: "If the man had ejaculated and then punched you, we'd have a shot at catching him. Just punched in the face, no semen." / "No semen." / "Story of my life."
jokes.setup: Following the semen database speech, Slater applies it practically to the case.
jokes.punchline: The victim's deadpan "story of my life" — implying his life is characterized by being punched without ejaculation — is the perfect absurdist button to Slater's clinical analysis.
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation and callback. 'No semen' repeated creates rhythm, and 'story of my life' is a killer button — the victim's delivery reframes the absurdity as mundane life disappointment. 'No semen. Story of my life' is extremely quotable. This two-joke sequence (14+15) together is among the episode's best.

jokes.text: "He's young, but the Force is strong with this one. Learning you are, young padawan." — Slater doing Star Wars voices unprompted to describe his new partner.
jokes.setup: Slater is explaining that Michaels is six months on the force and still learning.
jokes.punchline: He segues into Yoda-speak completely unprompted, mixing Star Wars references, and Michaels appears to genuinely enjoy it.
jokes.explanation: Lightly charming character moment — it establishes that Slater is a dork under the bluster — but Star Wars references as humor are well-worn and this doesn't add a twist. The 'Attack of the Clones' correction adds a mild beat but doesn't elevate it significantly.

jokes.text: "See, Michaels, you always take a call at a bar because better or worse, you get a beer out of it."
jokes.setup: A bar fight call comes in and Slater is explaining his philosophy of policing to Michaels.
jokes.punchline: His entire strategic rationale for responding to crime is free alcohol — delivered as genuine professional wisdom.
jokes.explanation: Good corrupt-cop character work. The fact that it's delivered as mentorship — genuine professional advice — makes it funnier than if it were a confession. The 'better or worse' hedge is a nice touch of fake balance.

jokes.text: "Set course for Bailey's, warp 10. Engage." — Slater invoking Star Trek to respond to the bar call.
jokes.setup: Following the Star Wars Yoda bit, Slater now switches to a Star Trek reference.
jokes.punchline: The switch from Star Wars to Star Trek (after Michaels corrected the Star Wars canon) adds a layer — Slater is an equal-opportunity sci-fi nerd — and the cop car becomes a starship.
jokes.explanation: Part of the nerd-cop running gag. Works better in context (after the Star Wars moment) than in isolation. 'Engage' is the right button word.

jokes.text: "Welcome to the Thunderdome." — Slater announcing their arrival at the bar.
jokes.setup: Cops arrive at the bar fight call.
jokes.punchline: Slater's pop-culture grandstanding — invoking Mad Max's Thunderdome for a bar brawl — is consistent with his character as a guy who performs being cool for himself.
jokes.explanation: Generic tough-guy pop culture quip. Fits character but adds little beyond basic texture. This is well below the semen-database or MySpace jokes in the same section.

jokes.text: "I'm essentially best friends with the guy... so a bunch of my buds are coming. We're gonna rock out with our cocks out. Just kidding. We are gonna rock out."
jokes.setup: Some random guy is leading Seth and Evan into what turns out to be a sketchy house party.
jokes.punchline: "Rock out with our cocks out" followed immediately by a nervous "Just kidding. We are gonna rock out" — the retreat makes it worse, not better.
jokes.explanation: "Rock out with our cocks out" is a well-worn phrase (it was already clichéd in 2007), but the "just kidding... we are gonna rock out" self-correction rescues it slightly. Mildly amusing, nothing special.

jokes.text: "This is something a smart person wouldn't do." — Seth's self-aware commentary on entering the sketchy party.
jokes.setup: Seth and Evan have arrived at a clearly sketchy house party in pursuit of alcohol.
jokes.punchline: Seth explicitly narrates his own bad decision-making — a moment of surprising self-awareness from a character usually defined by lack of it.
jokes.explanation: Good economy and slight subversion of Seth's usual bravado. Brief but effective. The understatement of "a smart person" does work.

jokes.text: "We should grab one of these buckets and get out." / "Are you out of your mind? How are we gonna get a fucking bucket out?"
jokes.setup: Seth and Evan are at the party scanning for alcohol.
jokes.punchline: The impracticality of stealing an entire bucket of alcohol — and Seth's oblivious certainty that it's a plan — contrasted with Evan's genuine logistical objection.
jokes.explanation: Good illustration of Seth's impulsive planning and Evan's straight-man role. 'How are we gonna get a fucking bucket out?' is a legitimately funny image — Evan is right, but it's the wrong question to ask here. Functional.

jokes.text: "You using my phone? You weren't invited. Get the fuck out of here... You calling your fucking friends again? You calling your friends, your fantastic friends?"
jokes.setup: Some random party host (Mark) confronts the uninvited guests.
jokes.punchline: The sarcastic "your fantastic friends" is weirdly poetic — an unexpected word choice — and the escalating repetition of the phone accusation suggests paranoid territorial logic.
jokes.explanation: "Your fantastic friends" lands as a funny incongruity — a weird, almost poetic insult in a drunken rage. The character is essentially unhinged aggression, which is funny but not brilliantly constructed.

jokes.text: "Tiger got out of the cage, man. All right? I'm sorry. Come on, Mark."
jokes.setup: Someone just punched Mark in the face, and the person responsible (or a bystander) is trying to de-escalate.
jokes.punchline: "Tiger got out of the cage" as an apology for punching someone is an absurdly self-aggrandizing excuse — framing an act of aggression as a force of nature he couldn't control.
jokes.explanation: "Tiger got out of the cage" is a nicely original self-mythologizing phrase — absurdly grandiose for a drunk punch at a house party. It's the kind of thing a certain type of person actually says, which makes it ring true.

jokes.text: "Right in the nads!" — Shouted as someone gets hit in the groin during the brawl.
jokes.setup: A fight has broken out at the party.
