jokes.punchline: "Right in the nads" — gleeful spectator commentary on a groin hit — is both a classic slapstick beat and funny for how enthusiastically it's announced.
jokes.explanation: Classic groin-hit comedy — lowest common denominator. It works in context because the enthusiasm is funny, but there's zero craft here. It's pure physical comedy with no twist.

jokes.text: "I need my nuts, man, for a lot of things."
jokes.setup: Seth is refusing to go back into the brawling party to steal liquor.
jokes.punchline: "I need my nuts for a lot of things" — the vague, earnest plural justification for protecting his genitals is funnier than any specific reason would have been.
jokes.explanation: "For a lot of things" is the key — the vagueness implies Seth has an entire planned life for which his testicles are essential and he doesn't care to specify. Perfect economy. Highly quotable. This is classic Superbad register.

jokes.text: "No, but I would get killed for pussy, no questions asked."
jokes.setup: Evan asks if Seth would risk getting hurt for liquor; Seth says no.
jokes.punchline: He immediately clarifies he WOULD get killed for sex — no questions asked — the reversal establishing his exact hierarchy of values.
jokes.explanation: Good reversal structure — not for liquor, but yes for sex, no questions. The moral hierarchy is funny and absolutely character-specific to Seth. "No questions asked" is the right emphatic button.

jokes.text: "Because I respect her, Seth. I'm not gonna put unfair pressure on her." — Evan's earnest explanation for why he hasn't made a move on Becca.
jokes.setup: Seth accuses Evan of being a "pussy" for not making a move on Becca despite liking her.
jokes.punchline: Evan's answer — "I respect her, I won't put unfair pressure on her" — is entirely sincere, which makes it funny in this context because it sounds like practiced therapy-speak from a 17-year-old, and also because his current plan involves getting her drunk.
jokes.explanation: Good character-specific irony. Evan's sincerity is funny on two levels: (1) he sounds like a guidance counselor at 17, and (2) the irony that he's literally trying to supply alcohol to this same girl. Works better in context of the full film.

jokes.text: "You pissed everywhere, you son of a bitch!" / "Everywhere? You didn't see me pissing anywhere. I don't know what you're talking about." / "Take your nuts out of your shells!"
jokes.setup: Cops arrive at Bailey's bar to find a full brawl in progress.
jokes.punchline: "Take your nuts out of your shells!" is a completely bizarre battle cry — a nonsense insult that lands as pure absurdism. The pissing denial despite evidence is also funny.
jokes.explanation: "Take your nuts out of your shells" is genuinely original — it's not a real expression, which makes it funnier. The pissing denial is a good cringe beat. Together these are chaotic bar energy that works.

jokes.text: "Should I shoot him?" / "No, no, no! No!" — Michaels asking for permission to shoot a fleeing bar patron.
jokes.setup: A suspect is fleeing the bar fight scene, and Michaels is in pursuit.
jokes.punchline: Michaels casually asks if he should shoot a fleeing bar-fight suspect — escalating from "arrest" to "execute" with zero proportionality — and Slater's panicked "No, no, no!" is the straight-man response.
jokes.explanation: Very sharp. The casual register of "should I shoot him?" — as if asking whether to hold the elevator — is the whole joke. It lands because Michaels has been established as eager and slightly unhinged. Dark, economical, character-specific. The repeated "No!" from Slater escalates it perfectly. Approaches the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: "Please stop it, you fucking bum. What the fuck?" — McLovin physically tackling the fleeing bar patron and immediately breaking character.
jokes.setup: Slater has yelled "McLovin, stop him!" and McLovin has apparently tackled the guy.
jokes.punchline: McLovin's takedown is immediately undercut by his own verbal reaction — "please stop it, you fucking bum" — which sounds like a frustrated librarian, not a hero cop.
jokes.explanation: "Please stop it, you fucking bum" is a great McLovin line — the "please" is the operative word, the politeness amid aggression. The gap between the heroic action (tackling a fleeing suspect) and his actual register (peeved and confused) is perfect character comedy.

jokes.text: "Hey. You dance hot." — A girl initiating conversation with Evan at a party.
jokes.setup: Evan is at the party, apparently having been dancing.
jokes.punchline: "You dance hot" is an oddly blunt compliment — syntactically off, delivered flatly — and sets up the period-blood reveal. In isolation it's a minor cringe beat.
jokes.explanation: More of a setup moment than a standalone joke, but the deadpan bluntness of "you dance hot" is mildly funny. Rewatch bonus because knowing what comes next makes the interaction funnier.

jokes.text: "Hey. Look what fell out of the truck!" — Fogell/McLovin's entrance with liquor.
jokes.setup: Seth and Evan had given up on getting alcohol and left the party.
jokes.punchline: McLovin announces his success by implying the alcohol fell off a truck — both a gag about how he obtained it and a classic euphemism for stolen goods — delivered with triumphant irony.
jokes.explanation: "Look what fell out of the truck" is a nicely compressed joke — invoking the "fell off a truck" euphemism for stolen goods, delivered as triumph. McLovin's "yeah, I know" follow-up deflates it slightly but adds a beat. Good economy.

jokes.text: "That fucking stain on your pants, idiot. What is that? Is that blood?"
jokes.setup: Seth notices something on Evan's pants after Evan was dancing with the girl.
jokes.punchline: The discovery of what appears to be blood on Evan's pants from the girl he was dancing with — setting up the period-blood sequence.
jokes.explanation: More of a setup than a joke in itself, but the reveal moment and Evan's confusion/horror are played well. The gradual realization structure works.

jokes.text: "Oh, fuck. Oh, my God." / "Someone perioded on my fucking leg?" — Evan's dawning horror upon realizing what the stain is.
jokes.setup: It's been established the stain is blood and Evan was dancing with a girl.
jokes.punchline: "Someone perioded on my fucking leg" — the verb "perioded" and the violation of personal space implied by menstrual blood on his pants — is an explosive, perfectly specific gross-out punchline.
jokes.explanation: "Someone perioded on my fucking leg" is one of the most quotable lines in the entire film. The coinage of 'perioded' as a verb is inspired — it's exactly the word a horrified 17-year-old would invent in the moment. The build (blood? you're bleeding? why would I be bleeding?) makes the payoff land with maximum impact. High craft, massive audience reaction. This is the standout gross-out joke of the reel.

jokes.text: "It's merlot. That's what you don't get." — Evan's desperate denial, claiming the period blood is red wine.
jokes.setup: Partygoers are gathering to point and laugh at Evan's stained pants.
jokes.punchline: Evan's specific wine-variety denial — not just "it's wine" but specifically "merlot" — is perfectly absurd. The specificity suggests he has thought this through, which only makes it worse.
jokes.explanation: "It's merlot. That's what you don't get." — the specificity of the varietal is what makes this exceptional. Any other word ("wine," "red wine," "cabernet") would be less funny. "Merlot" implies a weird dignity and connoisseurship in this deeply undignified moment. "That's what you don't get" adds a defensive superiority that's perfect character work. Extremely quotable.

jokes.text: "Oh, my God, that's a fucking man-gina, man. Do you need a tampon? I could... Wait, wait. I have one! I have one!"
jokes.setup: The crowd has gathered around Evan and his stained pants.
jokes.punchline: The crowd's escalating mockery — "man-gina," offering a tampon, then someone actually producing one — builds to absurdist heights, suggesting this person routinely carries tampons to deploy at moments like these.
jokes.explanation: The "I have one!" escalation — implying someone actually has a tampon ready — is the funniest beat here. The mockery is broad but lands because of the momentum from jokes 38-39.

jokes.text: "Yeah, I'm McLovin. I'd like to buy some..." — The cops watching and replaying McLovin's takedown on a security monitor, impersonating him.
jokes.setup: The cops are replaying bar security footage of McLovin's heroic tackle.
jokes.punchline: Slater impersonates McLovin's fake-ID voice from earlier in the film — calling back to McLovin's "I'm McLovin" persona — and the cops are gleefully rewinding it like a highlights reel.
jokes.explanation: Good callback that layers McLovin's identities — the bumbling fake-ID teenager and the accidental action hero. The cops treating the security footage like a touchdown replay is a nice absurdist touch.

jokes.text: "Your legs lifted off the ground. That is bona fide badass, man."
jokes.setup: The cops are reliving McLovin's tackle with genuine excitement.
jokes.punchline: The technical detail of "your legs lifted off the ground" as the specific evidence of badassery — combined with "bona fide" — is an overly formal compliment that's funny for its earnestness.
jokes.explanation: Pleasant supporting beat in the McLovin-cops bonding arc. "Bona fide badass" is a funny combination of formal and crude but not exceptional.

jokes.text: "The only thing that's evidence of is you can take a hit like a champ."
jokes.setup: McLovin asks if the cops need to keep the bar security footage as evidence.
jokes.punchline: Slater reframes the evidence question entirely — the tape isn't evidence of a crime, it's evidence of McLovin's toughness — which is both legally absurd and personally flattering in a way McLovin can't resist.
jokes.explanation: Good ironic logic. The cops' cavalier attitude to evidence destruction is funny in context of their overall corruption, and framing it as a McLovin compliment is a nice turn.

jokes.text: "You don't wanna meet a chick in a bar, man. Seriously. That was a turning point in my life... You gotta go to a spin class, a farmers' market, pumpkin patch, given the time of year."
jokes.setup: The cops are giving McLovin romantic advice.
jokes.punchline: "Pumpkin patch, given the time of year" — the specificity of seasonal availability for romance venues, as if Michaels has thought deeply about optimizing pick-up locations by calendar — is funny in its earnest detail.
jokes.explanation: Good cop-character specificity. The list (spin class, farmers' market, pumpkin patch) escalates in specificity until "pumpkin patch, given the time of year" lands as unexpectedly detailed advice. Solid.

jokes.text: "Yeah, I met the missus at paintball. Yeah, I shot her in the neck. And we just hit it off, you know."
jokes.setup: Michaels has recommended non-threatening social venues for meeting women. Slater chimes in with his own success story.
jokes.punchline: "I shot her in the neck. And we just hit it off" — the double meaning of "hit it off" (started a relationship / she was literally hit) is a good pun, but more importantly, paintball-to-romance via neck shot is an absurdly violent meet-cute.
jokes.explanation: Very good joke. The "hit it off" wordplay is clean, and the image of a romantic origin story starting with a paintball to the neck is perfectly absurd. Character-specific — only Slater would think this proves his point. The economy is good.

jokes.text: "My first wife... Who is a whore, by the way." — Slater's mid-sentence editorial insertion.
jokes.setup: Slater is about to contrast his current wife with his first wife.
jokes.punchline: The aside "who is a whore, by the way" is dropped as matter-of-fact parenthetical information — the "by the way" makes it funnier, as if he's helpfully providing a data point.
jokes.explanation: "Who is a whore, by the way" is a great character aside. The "by the way" transforms a bitter personal revelation into casual trivia. Extremely economical — four words do a lot. The casualness is the whole joke.

jokes.text: "Bought her a Binion's, complimented her on her tote bag... and next thing I know, she's putting her mouth around the tip of my penis."
jokes.setup: Slater is explaining how he met his first wife at this same bar.
jokes.punchline: The progression from a cheap drink and a compliment on a tote bag to explicit oral sex is jarring in its bluntness — the clinical "putting her mouth around the tip of my penis" is funnier for the precise anatomical specificity.
jokes.explanation: "The tip of my penis" is funnier than any cruder phrasing because of its clinical specificity — it sounds like a deposition. The escalation from "tote bag compliment" to this is a great structural leap. Good character voice.

jokes.text: "You don't have to tell me that."
jokes.setup: Slater has just described his first wife's oral sex act in clinical detail to a teenager.
jokes.punchline: McLovin's flat "you don't have to tell me that" is perfect — it's not angry, not shocked, just mildly protesting the overshare. The understatement of objecting to TMI from someone describing a sex act is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Perfect reaction beat. Five words that do maximum work: McLovin doesn't freak out, doesn't laugh — he just quietly protests, as if Slater has gone slightly too far at a dinner party. The deadpan understatement is impeccable economy and completely in character for McLovin.

jokes.text: "On our wedding night, we had group sex. I wasn't involved in it. But I could hear it through the wall." / "I was."
jokes.setup: Slater continues his first wife's story, noting she "opened up his world sexually."
jokes.punchline: "On our wedding night we had group sex. I wasn't involved in it" is a stunning escalation, and Michaels' casual "I was" — delivered as a simple factual addendum — is the perfect button.
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in this reel. The structure is flawless: setup (wedding night group sex), surprising reversal (I wasn't involved), and then Michaels' "I was" — a single word revelation that recontextualizes their entire relationship and implies a years-long backstory of betrayal delivered as a casual aside. The rhythm is perfect, the economy is extraordinary, and it's entirely character-specific. Comparable to the vasectomy anchor at 9+. The 'I was' is the whole movie.

jokes.text: "She was amazing. And then it was exactly 23 months later that I found out she was an actual whore. We discovered her on the street." / "Yeah."
jokes.setup: Following the wedding-night group sex reveal, Slater continues the story of his first marriage.
jokes.punchline: "An actual whore" — not figuratively but literally a sex worker — and "we discovered her on the street" implies they drove past her professionally working. "Exactly 23 months" adds a specific, almost obsessive precision to his memory of this betrayal.
jokes.explanation: "Exactly 23 months" is a precise, obsessive detail that characterizes Slater perfectly. "We discovered her on the street" — the 'we' implying Michaels was in the car when they found her — is a devastating callback to the 'I was' joke. The whole whore-wife arc is brilliantly sustained.

jokes.text: "And then it was exactly 23 months later that I found out she was an actual whore. We discovered her on the street."
jokes.setup: Slater has been building the story of his ex-wife
jokes.punchline: 'Actual whore' — she was literally a sex worker. 'We discovered her on the street.' The earlier parenthetical 'who is a whore, by the way' is now fully paid off: it was literal.
jokes.explanation: This is a callback payoff done exceptionally well. 'Who is a whore, by the way' was throwaway; 'actual whore' and 'we discovered her on the street' reveals it was literal the whole time. 'Exactly 23 months' — the precision of the number is funny in itself, suggesting Slater has replayed this timeline many times. 'We discovered her on the street' implies a genuine street-walking discovery, which is both darkly funny and weirdly clinical.

jokes.text: "Yeah, yeah, yeah. You'll meet her." — Slater to McLovin about his current wife, after the entire traumatic first-wife story.
jokes.setup: After the horrific first-wife story, Slater mentions his current wife is wonderful.
jokes.punchline: "You'll meet her" — delivered as if the first-wife story was just a brief tangent and they'll all be getting together for brunch — treats the deranged overshare as completely normal social context.
jokes.explanation: Good deadpan button on the first-wife sequence. "You'll meet her" implies a normalcy and future social relationship that is absurd given everything that just happened. Works well as a beat that closes the extended joke.

jokes.text: "She was bad. Fucking whoring bitch. / But you got a new wife now, so... / Yeah. Yeah. And she is wonderful. / You'll meet her."
jokes.setup: Slater has just finished his devastating ex-wife story
jokes.punchline: 'She was bad. Fucking whoring bitch.' delivered with real feeling — then immediately brightening to 'and she is wonderful. You'll meet her.' McLovin has apparently been invited to meet Slater's current wife
jokes.explanation: Good emotional whiplash — 'fucking whoring bitch' to 'you'll meet her' (re: the new wife) in three seconds. The invitation to McLovin to meet Slater's wife is an absurd overstep in familiarity for a man he met hours ago.

jokes.text: "It's not the going with the ladies I care about... it's the coming." — McLovin's sex pun, followed by a beat as the cops process it.
jokes.setup: The cops are asking McLovin how things are going with girls, expecting him to admit he's struggling.
jokes.punchline: McLovin subverts with a sex pun — "coming" — delivered with what appears to be both intentional wordplay and plausible deniability. The delay as the cops work it out is part of the joke.
jokes.explanation: "It's not the going with the ladies I care about, it's the coming" is a great McLovin joke because it's calibrated exactly to his character — just sophisticated enough to be intentional, just awkward enough that you can't be sure. The cop reaction ('I get it. What is it?') and then 'like coming' is a perfect reveal beat. High character integration — this joke lives in the gap between McLovin's social cluelessness and flashes of wit.

jokes.text: "That's funny. That is really funny." — Slater genuinely impressed by McLovin's coming/going joke, explaining it back
jokes.setup: McLovin has just made his coming/going pun
jokes.punchline: Slater and Michaels respond with over-the-top appreciation, with Slater needing to explain the joke back as if processing it — 'Like coming'
jokes.explanation: The cops over-explaining McLovin's joke back to itself ('Like: coming') while being deeply impressed is funny but subordinate to the original gag. The scene works as a unit.

jokes.text: "All right, looks like we got a call. We can't pay for these." / "We should get road beers." / "Hell, yeah, we should get some road beers. Can I have 13 beers to go, please?"
jokes.setup: The cops get an emergency call mid-beer at the bar.
jokes.punchline: Their response to an emergency call is to request 13 road beers and stiff the bar — these are law enforcement officers ordering to-go alcohol to drink in a squad car while responding to a 911 call.
jokes.explanation: "Can I have 13 beers to go, please?" — the specific number 13 is funny, and the "please" is a nice touch of absurd politeness in a corrupt act. Good character consistency but not a structurally exceptional joke.

jokes.text: "I was just calling, you know, to see if you were coming, because I thought maybe you were stuck at, like, a nightclub or a cocktail party or something."
jokes.setup: Evan has finally gotten through to Becca on the phone.
jokes.punchline: Becca imagines Evan might be delayed at "a nightclub or a cocktail party" — an utterly delusional picture of teenage Evan's social life, the gap between her fantasy and his actual night (bar brawl, period blood, etc.) is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Good ironic contrast — works on rewatch when you know what Evan's night has actually involved. The gap between Becca's imagined glamour and the chaotic reality is the comedic payload. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: "No, no, I'm gonna be there for sure. Full throttle. Charlie's Angels 2."
jokes.setup: Evan is trying to reassure Becca he'll make it to the party.
jokes.punchline: "Full throttle. Charlie's Angels 2" — two meaningless action-movie intensifiers deployed as confident reassurances. The randomness of "Charlie's Angels 2" specifically is an absurdist non-sequitur.
jokes.explanation: "Charlie's Angels 2" as a declaration of commitment is brilliantly random — why the sequel? The fact that it has absolutely no logical connection to the situation and Evan delivers it with apparent sincerity is the joke. Economical and original.

jokes.text: "That was the first time I ever did coke. Off that bitch's nipple. That was so... A little white sniff."
jokes.setup: Evan has just hung up with Becca and is now back in the crazy party context.
jokes.punchline: The immediate cut from Evan's innocent phone call to a random guy describing his first cocaine experience off a woman's nipple — the tonal whiplash is the primary comedic mechanism.
jokes.explanation: More of a tonal contrast/environment gag than a crafted joke. The world of this party is so depraved that random cocaine-nipple confessions are ambient noise. Works as atmosphere but not as a constructed joke.

jokes.text: "I've been praying for a fight. I'm literally waking up and praying to see a fucking fight."
jokes.setup: Someone mentions there might be a fight at the party tonight involving a jealous boyfriend.
jokes.punchline: This random person reveals he has been ritually praying each morning for the opportunity to witness a fight — suggesting it's a consistent spiritual practice.
jokes.explanation: "I literally wake up and pray for a fight" is a funny character moment — the religious devotion to witnessing violence as a lifestyle goal. Specific enough to feel real and original. Good.

jokes.text: "Who is that guy?" / "I'm nobody." — Fogell's instant denial to a room full of people who don't know him.
jokes.setup: McLovin enters the party and someone asks who he is.
jokes.punchline: "I'm nobody" — both a denial and an existential statement — is funnier because McLovin genuinely IS nobody at this party but has just been a hero to the cops.
jokes.explanation: Good economy. "I'm nobody" has depth — it's both social truth and ironic understatement given his recent cop-car adventure. Brief but effective.

jokes.text: "He's the guy with the beautiful voice. The fucking singer, Jimmy's brother!" — The party crowd insisting McLovin is a famous singer's brother.
jokes.setup: Earlier in the film McLovin was mistaken for someone named Jimmy's brother. Now it's happening again at a different party.
jokes.punchline: The callback to "Jimmy's brother" re-emerges here — McLovin's mysterious double continues to haunt him — escalating with "the beautiful voice" and demands that he sing.
jokes.explanation: Good callback that escalates — the confusion has followed McLovin to a new location, and now there's a whole mythology (the beautiful voice, Jimmy's brother from Scottsdale). The absurdity compounds well. Works better on rewatch.

jokes.text: "My brother came from Scottsdale, Arizona to be here. You're not gonna sing for him?"
jokes.setup: McLovin is being pressured to sing because they think he's Jimmy's brother.
jokes.punchline: The guilt trip about the brother coming from Scottsdale specifically — a specific, geographically far, slightly sad city — to see him perform is a great absurdist escalation.
jokes.explanation: "Scottsdale, Arizona" is a great specific choice — not New York, not LA, but Scottsdale: far enough to be meaningful, suburban enough to be pathetic. The escalation of the singer myth to include a devoted brother adds good absurdist detail.

jokes.text: "No, I don't mean to accuse you guys of being ill-informed, but..." — the stranger begins a formal objection to being misidentified
jokes.setup: The stranger is trying to deny being Jimmy's brother to increasingly insistent partygoers
jokes.punchline: 'I don't mean to accuse you guys of being ill-informed' — a bizarrely formal, diplomatic way to tell a drunk party crowd they're wrong about your identity
jokes.explanation: 'I don't mean to accuse you guys of being ill-informed' is a great formal register applied to a totally absurd situation. The character's attempt at diplomatic language in the middle of a chaotic party argument has a nice comic dignity to it.

jokes.text: "You want a line of cocaine? / No way, man. / Yeah." — cocaine offered as an incentive to sing
jokes.setup: Partygoers are trying to convince the stranger to sing; he keeps resisting
jokes.punchline: The final incentive offered is cocaine — matter-of-factly, as a reasonable inducement — and the stranger's 'no way, man' is met with 'yeah' as if cocaine was the obviously correct answer to his reluctance
jokes.explanation: Brief but effective — cocaine offered as a standard social negotiation chip. The deadpan 'yeah' response to 'no way, man' implies the offer is non-negotiable.

jokes.text: "0.08, motherfuckers!" — McLovin nailing the breathalyzer challenge.
jokes.setup: The cops and McLovin have been trying to blow exactly 0.08 on a breathalyzer as a game.
jokes.punchline: McLovin hits the exact legal limit on his first try and announces it triumphantly — a perfect absurdist sporting achievement.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character moment — McLovin's triumph is achieving the legal BAC limit, celebrated like a world record. "Motherfuckers" is the right level of uncharacteristic aggression for his celebration. The setup of multiple failed attempts makes the payoff earned. Great economy.

jokes.text: "It's like having two cocks. If one of your cocks could kill someone."
jokes.setup: McLovin asks what it's like to have a gun; Slater enthusiastically explains.
jokes.punchline: "Like having two cocks" is already a funny comparison, but "if one of your cocks could kill someone" — the conditional — is the actual punchline. It's absurd, slightly disturbing, and perfectly Slater.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in this reel. The two-step structure (like two cocks → but one could kill) is perfectly constructed. "If one of your cocks could kill someone" has an almost philosophical quality — it's a genuinely strange and original formulation. Very quotable. Slater-specific in its blend of machismo and absurdist logic.

jokes.text: "I shot that cat last week." / "It was already dead, man." / "I still shot it."
jokes.setup: Slater is challenging Michaels' marksmanship skills in front of McLovin.
jokes.punchline: Michaels' defense of his shooting ability is that he shot a dead cat. Slater's "it was already dead" destroys the defense, but Michaels doubles down with "I still shot it" — an absurdly minimal standard of achievement.
jokes.explanation: "I still shot it" is a brilliant punchline. The logic is perfect: Michaels is defending his competence with evidence of shooting a thing that required no skill to hit because it was stationary and dead — and his position is that this counts. The structure is clean three-line comedy, and "I still shot it" is the ideal deadpan button. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: "Shoot-off. Shoot-off. Shoot-off!" — Spontaneous escalation into a shoot-off contest between the cops.
jokes.setup: The dead-cat argument has established a marksmanship dispute.
jokes.punchline: Both cops immediately escalate to demanding a shoot-off — the problem-solving logic of two cops with guns settling their competence debate the same way cowboys would.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation beat — the inevitability of the shoot-off is funny, and both cops agreeing instantly suggests it's how they normally settle disputes. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: "Mark. Mark, that's him. Johnny Cash. Right there. Oh, you got a stain too. We're blood brothers."
jokes.setup: During the shoot-off conversation, Evan is spotted by the jealous boyfriend (referred to as Johnny Cash).
jokes.punchline: The guy who has period blood on his pants refers to the jealous boyfriend as having "a stain too" and declares them "blood brothers" — an absurd bond formed over menstrual blood on pants.
jokes.explanation: "We're blood brothers" is a great callback to the period-blood sequence. The double meaning of "blood brothers" (actual blood, menstrual blood, male bonding ritual) works on multiple levels. The "shut the fuck up" response deflates it perfectly.

jokes.text: "No, I wasn't dancing. I don't even dance. That's the thing. I've never tried it. So it's weird that you'd think that." — Evan explaining to the jealous boyfriend that he wasn't dancing.
jokes.setup: An angry guy (the fiancée of the girl Evan was dancing with) confronts Evan.
jokes.punchline: Evan's denial escalates into a philosophical statement about his entire relationship with dance — "I've never tried it" — which is transparently false and comically overcomplicated as a denial.
jokes.explanation: "I don't even dance. That's the thing. I've never tried it." is a great escalating lie — the more he insists, the more elaborate and implausible it becomes. "So it's weird that you'd think that" is the perfect final note of accusation-reversal. Good character-specific cringe.

jokes.text: I got fucking blood on my pants.
jokes.setup: Chaos is erupting at a house party — a full fight has broken out, people are fleeing, cops are being called.
jokes.punchline: Seth's singular concern amid total mayhem is that he got blood on his pants — a perfect encapsulation of his self-centered priorities.
jokes.explanation: The joke works because of perfect economy and character specificity — Seth's obliviousness to danger in favor of his own trivial inconvenience is very on-brand. It lands as a character beat more than a crafted punchline.

jokes.text: Oh, shit, I've been tackled by little girls!
jokes.setup: A fight is breaking out at the party; someone has been tackled to the ground.
jokes.punchline: The tackler turns out to be small girls, which the man finds more humiliating than the tackle itself.
jokes.explanation: Functional slapstick with a mild subversion. The humor comes from wounded masculine pride, which is a familiar but reliably funny beat. Not especially crafted, but gets the job done.

jokes.text: You used my leg as a tampon!
jokes.setup: A man is furious at another person who apparently got menstrual blood on his pants during the chaotic party.
jokes.punchline: The accusation 'you used my leg as a tampon' is grotesque, specific, and escalates the confrontation to an absurd level of indignation.
jokes.explanation: One of the more inventive insults in the reel. 'You used my leg as a tampon' is specific, visceral, and genuinely surprising — the audience doesn't expect this escalation. The image is so absurd and specific that it becomes highly quotable. Strong originality score because this phrasing is not a stock insult.

jokes.text: Mark, I called the cops. You should hide your gun.
jokes.setup: Someone has called the cops on the chaotic party; a person named Mark is apparently armed.
jokes.punchline: The utterly calm, friendly advice to 'hide your gun' because cops are coming reveals the insane normality of gun ownership in this environment — delivered as if it's the most routine suggestion.
jokes.explanation: The deadpan delivery of this advice is the entire joke — the casual normalization of a friend having a gun and needing to hide it from police is darkly funny. Good economy, strong structure.

jokes.text: Oh, suck on my nuts, Slater!
jokes.setup: Officers Slater and Michaels are messing around with a gun at the party, apparently shooting at something for fun.
jokes.punchline: Michaels trash-talks his partner with gleeful vulgarity after making a shot — the juvenile behavior from law enforcement officers is the core joke.
jokes.explanation: Works primarily as character comedy — the joke is that these are cops behaving like frat boys. The line itself isn't particularly inventive but fits the duo's arrested-development dynamic.

jokes.text: I got jizzed on. All right.
jokes.setup: In the chaotic party aftermath, Slater casually announces he got ejaculate on him.
jokes.punchline: The 'All right.' that follows is the entire punchline — the total acceptance of this outrageous situation as just another thing that happened tonight.
jokes.explanation: The deadpan resignation is what makes this funny. 'All right.' after announcing you've been jizzed on is perfect economy — the character has decided this is simply not a big deal tonight, which is funnier than any outrage would be.

jokes.text: Shotgun. [beat — Michaels calls shotgun after the car has already been claimed and everyone has fled]
jokes.setup: Everyone scrambles for the police cruiser yelling 'Shotgun! Shotgun! Bail!' in a panic.
jokes.punchline: After all the chaos has subsided and they're presumably in the car, one character quietly says 'Shotgun.' — the belated, unnecessary call in the stillness after the storm.
jokes.explanation: A quiet callback beat that works entirely on timing and deflation. After the frantic 'Shotgun! Shotgun!' scramble, the lone quiet 'Shotgun.' in the aftermath is a perfect comedic exhale. The rewatch bonus is earned because you notice it more on subsequent viewings.

jokes.text: You're fucking living the dream, Michaels!
jokes.setup: The cops have just fled a chaotic party they caused/joined, McLovin is in their car, they're supposed to be working.
jokes.punchline: Slater's sincere congratulation to Michaels for this absurd debauchery treats the whole disaster as an achievement — the irony that this IS the dream for these cops.
jokes.explanation: Works because it's both ironic and sincere — Slater genuinely means it, and that sincerity is funnier than pure sarcasm would be. Good character integration for the delinquent cop duo.

jokes.text: Hey, did she say we're gonna get to shoot somebody or something? / Oh, God, I wish.
jokes.setup: The dispatcher has radioed in a call; the cops are heading to a house party.
jokes.punchline: Slater's 'Oh, God, I wish' response to whether they'll get to shoot someone reveals a genuinely disturbing enthusiasm for gun violence — played for laughs as character-defining corruption.
jokes.explanation: Strong character integration — this two-line exchange perfectly defines both cops. Michaels is naive-dumb, Slater is gleefully corrupt. 'Oh, God, I wish' is a great punchline because of how casually monstrous it is. The dark subversion lands because of the commitment to character.

jokes.text: It's probably some lame house party. We'll drop you off after. Cool?
jokes.setup: Slater and Michaels are on-duty police officers responding to a call, with McLovin riding along.
jokes.punchline: Slater treats the police call like a minor errand he needs to run before getting back to hanging out — the casual inversion of police duty as an inconvenience.
jokes.explanation: Another solid piece of character comedy for the delinquent cops. The joke is in the inversion of priorities — a police call is the minor inconvenience, and their social time with McLovin is the priority.

jokes.text: You fucking prick. / What?
jokes.setup: Seth and Evan are walking after the party chaos; there's clearly tension between them.
jokes.punchline: Seth's completely genuine 'What?' — as if he has no idea why he might be called a prick — lands as perfect oblivious character comedy.
jokes.explanation: The 'What?' is funnier than the insult because it's so genuinely bewildered. Seth's obliviousness is a consistent character trait and this is a good quick expression of it.

jokes.text: I'm not gonna let you slow me down anymore, Seth.
jokes.setup: Evan and Seth are having a drunken emotional argument about Evan getting into Dartmouth and Seth feeling abandoned.
jokes.punchline: Evan drops a genuinely brutal, cold dismissal on his best friend — the emotional honesty is so raw and uncomfortable that it goes beyond drama into cringe comedy.
jokes.explanation: This scene functions as cringe comedy — the audience is uncomfortable and amused simultaneously. The specific line is funny-painful because Evan has clearly been holding this in and it comes out with devastating precision. Part of the sustained comedic discomfort of the argument section.

jokes.text: Instead of chasing girls and making friends, I've just sat around wasting all my time with you. And now I'm going to college a fucking friendless virgin.
jokes.setup: Evan's escalating drunk emotional outburst against Seth — the argument has been building.
jokes.punchline: 'Friendless virgin' is the kicker that tips the genuine emotional complaint into comedy — the self-own embedded in the attack on Seth.
jokes.explanation: Strong character integration — the joke only works because Evan is so earnest and self-unaware. He's trying to wound Seth but inadvertently reveals himself. The pivot from accusation to self-pity in 'going to college a fucking friendless virgin' is genuinely well-constructed and character-specific.

jokes.text: Is this about Becca? This is about some girl, man? / I like her! / Who gives a fuck? She's some fucking girl!
jokes.setup: Evan has been pouring his heart out about friendship and loneliness; Seth pivots to dismiss it all as being about a girl.
jokes.punchline: Seth's reductive 'Who gives a fuck? She's some fucking girl!' completely missing Evan's emotional point — while also ironically being exactly what Seth does care about — is excellent character comedy.
jokes.explanation: Seth's hypocrisy is the core of the joke — this entire night has been about Seth trying to get laid, and now he's dismissing Evan's feelings about a girl. Strong character integration because only Seth could be this oblivious and hypocritical in the same breath.

jokes.text: Hey, McLovin, are the numbers on your side odd or even? / I don't know. It's too dark to see. / We got flashlights.
jokes.setup: In the middle of a highly charged emotional fight between Seth and Evan, we cut to the cops' car where Slater asks McLovin about house numbers.
jokes.punchline: The complete tonal non-sequitur — moving from the boys' raw emotional fight to this mundane cop logistics exchange — is the joke. The juxtaposition deflates the drama perfectly.
jokes.explanation: The edit is the punchline — the script uses the intercut structure to comic effect. The mundanity of 'We got flashlights' as a response to the boys' screaming emotional crisis is structurally very funny. The scene break here is doing real comedic work.

jokes.text: Now, young Michaels, you will die.
jokes.setup: The cops are goofing around, shining flashlights at each other in the dark.
jokes.punchline: Slater's mock-villain declaration 'Now, young Michaels, you will die' — the theatrical performance for no audience — reveals these cops are essentially big children.
jokes.explanation: Decent character moment reinforcing that the cops are immature. The 'young Michaels' flourish is a nice touch. Not especially original but works in the rhythm of the scene.

jokes.text: Why did you do that? My God. / Are you guys gonna make sure he's okay?
jokes.setup: Seth and Evan's physical fight has apparently resulted in someone being hurt — context suggests one of them knocked the other down or into something.
jokes.punchline: The cops' response to apparently injuring someone (or witnessing the boys injure each other near the police car) — asking if they should check on him as if it's optional — is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Functional beat — the cops' casual indifference to injury reinforces their negligence as a running character trait. Not a standout joke but serves the scene rhythm.

jokes.text: Balls. Okay, we'll both go out there and check on him.
jokes.setup: Slater and Michaels debate who has to go check on the person who was apparently hit; neither wants to.
jokes.punchline: 'Balls.' as a resigned expletive before agreeing to do the responsible thing — the 'Balls.' is a perfect microcosm of Michaels' entire character.
jokes.explanation: One word — 'Balls.' — does enormous character work. It's the sound of a man who knows he has to do the right thing and hates it. The economy here is excellent; the character specificity is high.

jokes.text: I can't believe this is happening again. What are the odds?
jokes.setup: The police cruiser has apparently hit someone (or come close to it) — referencing an earlier incident in the film where they hit someone with their car.
jokes.punchline: Slater treats a potential vehicular incident as a statistical improbability rather than a consequence of his terrible driving/policing — 'What are the odds?' as genuine bewilderment.
jokes.explanation: Strong callback that earns its laugh by assuming the audience remembers the earlier incident. 'What are the odds?' is perfect character comedy — Slater genuinely cannot connect cause and effect. The rewatch bonus applies because the callback deepens on second viewing. Scores high because the character logic is airtight.

jokes.text: Is everyone okay? / Yeah, we're great, thanks.
jokes.setup: The cops have apparently just hit or nearly hit the boys with their car.
jokes.punchline: The sarcastic 'Yeah, we're great, thanks' from the nearly-run-over teen is a perfect deadpan retort to the absurdly cheerful police inquiry.
jokes.explanation: Competent sarcastic retort. Works in context, not especially memorable, but gets a mild laugh from the irony.

jokes.text: Hey, hey, where's the love?
jokes.setup: The cops have just nearly run over the boys and are now acting as if everything is fine.
jokes.punchline: Michaels' 'Where's the love?' — expecting warmth from people he just almost killed — is a perfect expression of his oblivious friendliness.
jokes.explanation: Good character beat. Michaels' eagerness for approval and affection while being completely oblivious to his own culpability is a consistent and funny character trait.

jokes.text: Spread your shit! Pussies on the pavement, fellas.
jokes.setup: Slater is performing a police stop on Seth and Evan
jokes.punchline: 'Pussies on the pavement' as an invented/non-standard police command — Slater has made up his own jargon
jokes.explanation: 'Pussies on the pavement' is a genuinely funny invention — it sounds like a police command but is completely unprofessional. The specificity of this invented jargon is what makes it work over generic cop-improvising-authority.

jokes.text: I am the law! Okay? Now hold hands.
jokes.setup: Slater has been screaming authority at the boys — 'Spread your shit! Get on the ground! I am the law!' — establishing maximum aggression.
jokes.punchline: The pivot from maximum aggression to 'Now hold hands' is a perfect, absurd non-sequitur that completely undercuts his authority display.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The setup is perfect — Slater has been performing maximum authority with increasingly ridiculous proclamations ('Spread your shit! Pussies on the pavement!'), building the audience's expectation for more aggression. 'Now hold hands' is the perfect subversion: it's controlling, humiliating, and yet weirdly gentle. The structure is clean, the punchline is memorable, and it's deeply character-specific — only this particular brand of unhinged cop would think of this. High quotability because it's unexpected and short.

jokes.text: What? / Why? [the boys reacting to being told to hold hands]
jokes.setup: Slater has just ordered the boys, who are in the middle of a heated fight with each other, to hold hands.
jokes.punchline: The genuine confusion/horror from boys who hate each other right now at being forced into physical intimacy with each other is the visual reaction beat.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the fight makes this land harder — these two were just screaming at each other, and now they have to hold hands under duress. The layering of the emotional context onto the physical absurdity is what elevates this beyond a simple reaction beat.

jokes.text: You don't want an asshole where your face used to be, Whaling Jennings.
jokes.setup: Seth or Evan has apparently balked at the hand-holding order.
jokes.punchline: The threat 'you don't want an asshole where your face used to be' is both viscerally threatening and anatomically absurd — and 'Whaling Jennings' as a made-up tough-guy address name is a perfect non-sequitur.
jokes.explanation: Two jokes packed into one line: (1) the anatomically impossible yet viscerally threatening image of having an asshole where your face used to be, and (2) 'Whaling Jennings' — a completely invented tough-cop nickname that sounds real but isn't. Both are highly original. The combination makes this one of the reel's standout lines. Slater's specific brand of unhinged authority is perfectly expressed.

jokes.text: Hold his fucking hand! / Fucking hold my hand.
jokes.setup: The boys are reluctant to hold hands; the cop is insisting with increasing forcefulness.
jokes.punchline: The escalation of authority — a cop screaming 'Hold his fucking hand!' — over such a minor, strange request is perfectly disproportionate and funny.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the hand-holding sequence is working as a sustained cringe beat. 'Fucking hold my hand' from the reluctant boy is the best part — the resignation to this absurd humiliation.

jokes.text: Here, McLovin, have a cigarette. Smoke up. Life's short, you know. Suck it in, my friend. Suck it long and deep.
jokes.setup: While Slater intimidates the boys, Michaels is hanging out with McLovin like a cool older brother figure.
jokes.punchline: Michaels giving a minor a cigarettes with the life-advice 'Life's short' while his partner terrorizes the kid's friends is an excellent contrast. 'Suck it long and deep' as parting wisdom is unintentionally homoerotic and absurd.
jokes.explanation: The contrast between good-cop Michaels and bad-cop Slater is funny here — Michaels is corrupting McLovin in his own gentle way. 'Suck it long and deep' as cigarette advice lands as unintentionally inappropriate, adding an extra layer.

jokes.text: McLovin, McLovin, McLovin. / You like Officer Slater and myself? / Yeah, you guys are awesome. / Thanks. We really like you too, McLovin.
jokes.setup: The cops have just terrorized two teenagers and are now asking McLovin for his approval.
jokes.punchline: The mutual appreciation society between the delinquent cops and McLovin — 'We really like you too, McLovin' — said with complete sincerity after acts of police misconduct, is funny because of the total inversion of authority and the genuine neediness of the cops.
jokes.explanation: The cops needing McLovin's validation is a consistent and funny dynamic. The warmth is genuine, which makes it funnier than if it were sarcastic.

jokes.text: So here's what's about to happen. We're gonna arrest these guys, you're gonna write a witness report saying they leapt in front of our car and there was nothing we could do. Sound cool?
jokes.setup: Slater has been acting as if he has some authority over McLovin; now he reveals the actual plan.
jokes.punchline: Slater's matter-of-fact conspiracy proposal — asking a teenager to falsify police reports as if it's a totally normal request — culminating in the casual 'Sound cool?' is excellent.
jokes.explanation: 'Sound cool?' is the perfect button on a genuinely dark bit. Slater is asking a 17-year-old to commit obstruction of justice and frames it as a fun collaborative activity. The casualness is the joke, and it's deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: So here's what's about to happen. We're gonna arrest these guys, you're gonna write a witness report saying they leapt in front of our car...
jokes.setup: Slater is now explaining the plan — the cops are going to frame Seth and Evan for jumping in front of the car
jokes.punchline: The casualness with which Slater explains evidence fabrication — 'sound cool?' — as if proposing a fun social activity rather than a crime
jokes.explanation: 'Sound cool?' after proposing witness report falsification to a minor is excellent. The casualness is the joke — Slater treats evidence tampering like asking someone if they want to grab food.

jokes.text: That's good. Pretend he's your little sister. Your little sister with the...
jokes.setup: Michaels is coaching one of the boys on how to hold the other's hand, trying to make the forced hand-holding less uncomfortable.
jokes.punchline: The sentence trails off — 'Your little sister with the...' — Michaels apparently can't finish whatever inappropriate thought he was about to have about a little sister. The unfinished sentence is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best jokes because of what ISN'T said. The unfinished sentence 'Your little sister with the...' forces the audience to complete it themselves, and wherever their imagination goes is funnier than anything that could have been said. The structure is perfect: build, build, trail off. The trailing off IS the punchline. High economy score because Michaels' unhinged personality does all the work. Rewatch bonus because you catch new implications each time.

jokes.text: Fagell? [cops realize McLovin is Fogell, a person they presumably know or have on file]
jokes.setup: Slater has been treating McLovin as a cool new friend named McLovin; he now apparently recognizes the name or face as belonging to Fogell.
jokes.punchline: The recognition that McLovin is actually Fogell — a known quantity — reframes everything about their relationship and presumably reveals that the fake ID was for someone they know.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that the cops now know McLovin is actually Fogell is a good narrative beat that works comedically from the irony of the situation. The rewatch bonus applies because the whole evening's interactions are recontextualized.

jokes.text: That was a fast kid.
jokes.setup: McLovin has apparently just fled from the cops at high speed; they've failed to catch him.
jokes.punchline: After a chase scene, Michaels' only observation is the deadpan, matter-of-fact 'That was a fast kid.' — as if speed was the only notable element of their failure.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — five words that do enormous comedic work. Michaels' ability to respond to chaos with complete understatement is the character's signature, and this is one of its best expressions. 'That was a fast kid.' accepts defeat with the equanimity of someone describing weather.

jokes.text: I want a ride! You hear me? You can't unarrest me!
jokes.setup: The boys have apparently been 'arrested' by the cops and are now being abandoned as the cops chase McLovin.
jokes.punchline: 'You can't unarrest me!' — the protest that one's arrest status cannot be retroactively revoked — is a great comic invention. The word 'unarrest' doesn't exist and that's what makes it funny.
jokes.explanation: 'You can't unarrest me!' is one of the most quotable lines in this reel. The invention of 'unarrest' as a word reveals a character who is both outraged and legally confused. It's a genuine comic coinage — the character believes he has accumulated an arrest status that can't simply be taken away. High quotability because the word is both funny and oddly logical.

jokes.text: McLovin! McLovin! Why?
jokes.setup: McLovin has fled the cops and they're calling after him in distress.
jokes.punchline: 'Why?' — Slater's heartbroken question after McLovin's betrayal is genuine and that sincerity is what makes it funny. He's treating McLovin's escape as a personal betrayal of their friendship.
jokes.explanation: The comedy comes from the genuine emotional investment Slater has in McLovin. 'Why?' is a one-word expression of betrayal that works because of everything we've seen in their earlier friendship scenes. Good character integration.

jokes.text: My hand! Monster! Nicole! Nicole, get Daddy. / Get Daddy! / Oh, shit. / Get away from my kids!
jokes.setup: The chase has apparently brought the cops into a residential area where someone is innocently outside with their children.
jokes.punchline: A man screaming for his daughter to 'Get Daddy' while apparently getting his hand hurt — and a child named Nicole screaming 'Get Daddy!' in echo — in the middle of the cops' McLovin chase is chaotic slapstick escalation.
jokes.explanation: Physical chaos escalation that works as a quick beat but isn't especially crafted. The confusion of 'Get Daddy' as a command spoken to Daddy himself is a mild funny confusion, but it's mostly just chaotic noise. Functional.

jokes.text: It's just beer. / Give me a break. / It's just beer. / Man up.
jokes.setup: Michaels or one of the boys is apparently upset/wet from something; the response is that it's 'just beer.'
jokes.punchline: The repeated 'It's just beer' as dismissal of genuine distress — and 'Man up' — from the same cops who were crying about McLovin running away thirty seconds ago.
jokes.explanation: Decent beat that plays on the irony of these particular authority figures dispensing 'man up' advice. Not especially memorable but works in context.

jokes.text: He's the fastest kid alive. / This is not good. / He's the fastest kid alive.
jokes.setup: The cops have failed to catch McLovin and are strategizing.
jokes.punchline: Michaels repeating 'He's the fastest kid alive' as if this is a settled scientific fact — twice — reduces the problem to this one immovable truth that cannot be overcome.
jokes.explanation: The repetition is what makes it — 'He's the fastest kid alive' the second time is funnier than the first because Michaels has apparently decided this is simply true and cannot be argued with. The escalation from 'that was a fast kid' to 'the fastest kid alive' is a nice progression.

jokes.text: I'll shoot my gun in the air. / Give me a fucking warning before you do it. / I'll scare him out of wherever he's hiding.
jokes.setup: The cops are discussing how to find McLovin; Michaels proposes shooting his gun.
jokes.punchline: Slater's only objection to randomly discharging a firearm in a residential area is 'Give me a fucking warning' — not concern for public safety, just personal inconvenience. The plan itself (scare him out of hiding by shooting) is treated as reasonable.
jokes.explanation: Slater's objection is entirely about his own comfort rather than the many obvious objections to randomly shooting a gun in public. This is a perfect character joke — his corrupt cop logic is internally consistent and therefore funnier.

jokes.text: Oh, fuck. Oh, fuck. They shot Seth. They fucking shot Seth, I know it.
jokes.setup: Gunshots have been fired nearby; Evan doesn't know what's happening.
jokes.punchline: Evan's immediate certainty that 'they fucking shot Seth, I know it' — the leap from hearing a gunshot to the most dramatic conclusion — is funny because of how certain and specific the assumption is.
jokes.explanation: 'I know it' is the key — Evan's certainty is what makes it funny. He has no evidence but absolute conviction. Good beat for his character, though not particularly inventive.

jokes.text: Hey, Evan, pay for me, please.
jokes.setup: Seth and Evan have just fled a terrifying situation involving cops and gunshots; they've managed to get on a bus.
jokes.punchline: Seth's first words after the chaos subsides are asking Evan to pay his bus fare — establishing that he never has money and that Seth's mind immediately goes to petty practical inconveniences.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character economy. After running from cops and near-gunshots, Seth's concern is bus fare. This is exactly the kind of mundane pivot that reveals character with maximum efficiency.

jokes.text: McMuffin. / Ain't got no cop people to help you keep your booze now, do you?
jokes.setup: An antagonist from earlier in the film recognizes Fogell/McLovin on the bus.
jokes.punchline: 'McMuffin' as a mangled version of McLovin is funny on its own, and 'cop people' as a description of his police escort is a perfect street-logic phrasing.
jokes.explanation: 'McMuffin' is a genuinely funny mis-remembering of the name, and 'cop people' has a great rhythm. The callback works because it confirms that McLovin's police adventure was visible to this antagonist.

jokes.text: Goldslick. [the antagonist is eventually repelled]
jokes.setup: The confrontation on the bus ends when the antagonist is apparently forced off or backs down.
jokes.punchline: The final word from the antagonist as he retreats — a parting insult or expression that is a made-up word — landing as an absurd final word in the conflict.
jokes.explanation: Minor laugh — the invented word as final insult works as an absurdist button on the confrontation. Not particularly crafted but functional.

jokes.text: Eat shit, bum.
jokes.setup: The drunk antagonist has been expelled from the bus; Seth delivers a parting shot.
jokes.punchline: 'Eat shit, bum.' — the casual authority of this dismissal from a teenage boy who seconds ago was cowering — is funny because of the confidence gap.
jokes.explanation: Three words that reveal Seth perfectly — the bravado that emerges only once danger has passed. Classic character comedy with great economy.

jokes.text: Yeah, I told you the idea would work. I fooled those cops. I'm McLovin. I am McLovin.
jokes.setup: They've made it to the party with the booze; Fogell is taking credit for the successful night.
jokes.punchline: Fogell claiming he 'fooled those cops' — when in fact the cops were actively helping him all night — is a perfect ironic self-delusion. 'I am McLovin' as a declaration of identity is also funny because we know the whole ID is a fraud.
jokes.explanation: Strong character comedy — Fogell's self-mythology is at the core of his character. 'I fooled those cops' is a magnificent ironic statement since the cops were essentially his accomplices. 'I am McLovin' has become a cultural touchstone of the film, and the moment here captures the character's complete absorption into his fake identity.

jokes.text: Why do you guys have detergent?
jokes.setup: The detergent was established at the opening of this reel (62:28) as something Seth inexplicably had during the party chaos.
jokes.punchline: McLovin asking about the detergent only now — after all the chaos — highlights that this strange detail has been carried through the entire adventure and nobody explained it.
jokes.explanation: A good callback that earns a rewatch bonus — on first viewing you've probably forgotten the detergent, so this question is both funny in itself and makes you re-examine the earlier scene.

jokes.text: Because I fucking rule.
jokes.setup: Evan questions why McLovin was smoking cigarettes with the cops.
jokes.punchline: 'Because I fucking rule.' — the unearned but completely sincere self-assessment — is the perfect Fogell/McLovin answer. It explains nothing while being entirely self-consistent.
jokes.explanation: Four words that are essentially the McLovin character thesis statement. The gap between his self-perception and reality is the entire joke, and 'Because I fucking rule' captures it perfectly. High character integration because this exact line couldn't come from Seth or Evan — only someone who has fully committed to a fake identity would answer this way.

jokes.text: I can't believe Becca's bottle broke. / I'm sure it'll be fine. / Yeah. / I thought you didn't need it. You were gonna tell her how you feel.
jokes.setup: Evan had earlier presumably claimed he didn't need alcohol to talk to Becca — that he'd just be honest with her.
jokes.punchline: Fogell calling Evan out on his brave declaration now that the safety net (Becca's alcohol) is gone — delivered as a mock-cheerful reminder.
jokes.explanation: A functional callback that exposes Evan's hypocrisy. Not especially inventive but serves the character dynamic well.

jokes.text: Good luck getting Jules drunk enough to have sex with you.
jokes.setup: The boys are discussing their plans for the party; McLovin comments on Seth's chances with Jules.
jokes.punchline: McLovin casually articulating Seth's actual strategy — that Jules needs to be drunk to have sex with Seth — said to Seth's face without any apparent awareness of how terrible this is.
jokes.explanation: Dark subversion that works because it's delivered by McLovin with casual matter-of-factness. The joke lands on the uncomfortable truth — but the film is leaning into the dark edge of teenage male thinking, which Superbad does throughout.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, Fogell's rooming with Evan. Jeez, why don't you go cry about it?
jokes.setup: It's been revealed that Evan and Fogell are rooming together at college; Seth is told this news.
jokes.punchline: Seth's immediate dismissal — 'Why don't you go cry about it?' — when he is CLEARLY the one who is devastated, delivered with false bravado, is a perfect ironic self-betrayal.
jokes.explanation: Classic dramatic irony — 'Why don't you go cry about it?' from someone who clearly wants to cry about it. Seth's denial makes the joke, and his character voice is perfectly captured. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: I didn't expect this from you, Evan. Not from you.
jokes.setup: Seth has been acting unconcerned about the Fogell/Evan rooming news, then pivots to deeply wounded.
jokes.punchline: The theatrical betrayal — 'Not from you.' — is so overwrought that it becomes comedic. Seth's emotional investment in Evan is played as comically excessive.
jokes.explanation: The 'Not from you' pause-and-add is a great comedic structure — the extra beat of 'Not from you' after the main sentence lands as comedically excessive emotional performance. Character-specific because only Seth would be this melodramatic.

jokes.text: Give me that booze, Fagell. [Seth takes the booze and walks away with dignity]
jokes.setup: Seth has just had an emotional revelation about being left behind; he needs an exit.
jokes.punchline: Taking the booze and walking away as his only response — the booze as emotional consolation prize and face-saving exit — is a perfect Seth moment.
jokes.explanation: Physical character beat — Seth's dignity requires him to walk away with something, and the booze is both practical and symbolic. 'Fagell' as his chosen form of address in the moment of emotional defeat is perfect.

jokes.text: She's way smashed. And she's been yammering about you all night. / Really? What was she saying? / She told you that she thinks I'm a good guy? / No, no. She said something more like: 'I will fully blow him tonight.'
jokes.setup: Evan is told that Becca has been talking about him; he immediately assumes the content was sweet and complimentary, anticipating something romantic.
jokes.punchline: 'I will fully blow him tonight' subverts Evan's self-insert romantic narrative with graphic directness — 'fully blow him' as a phrase is funny because of the word 'fully', which makes it sound like a formal commitment.
jokes.explanation: Strong misdirection — the structure is clean (Evan's romantic interpretation is set up, then demolished). 'I will fully blow him tonight' is funny because of 'fully' — it sounds like a contract rather than desire. The setup through Evan's hopeful self-delusion makes the punchline land harder.

jokes.text: But she's totally hammered and if I get with her and I'm not drunk, isn't that unethical? / Not if you're drunk too.
jokes.setup: Evan is being told that Becca wants him; he has a sudden ethical concern.
jokes.punchline: Gaby's 'Not if you're drunk too' as a solution to the ethical problem of pursuing a drunk person — the logic that mutual intoxication solves consent issues — is both a great character joke and a sharp piece of dark comedy.
jokes.explanation: One of the more sharply written exchanges in the reel. Gaby's response is both funny as a logical non-solution and revealing of teenage ethics. The economy is excellent — the entire joke lives in the five-word punchline. The film is aware of the dark subtext here, which is what makes it comedy rather than endorsement.

jokes.text: To Seth. / To Seth! / Who the fuck is Seth? / I'm Seth! / Let's do another one to me.
jokes.setup: Evan toasts to Seth at a party where nobody knows them.
jokes.punchline: 'Who the fuck is Seth?' from a party guest — establishing that Seth's grand entrance and self-importance is unknown to literally everyone here — followed by Seth's delighted 'I'm Seth! Let's do another one to me!' is a perfect character beat.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure — the setup (toast to Seth), the deflation (who the fuck is Seth), and the perfect response (I'm Seth! Let's do another one to me!) create a three-beat joke that lands hard. Seth's complete lack of embarrassment and immediate capitalization on the situation is deeply character-specific. 'Let's do another one to me' is a great quotable line because of its unselfconscious narcissism.

jokes.text: Calm down. Calm down, man. / Calm down. She likes you. / She wants to suck on your penis. / It's a good thing. / It's the best thing.
jokes.setup: Seth is apparently freaking out about Jules/Becca liking him; his friends are trying to calm him down.

jokes.explanation: Good escalation structure — the comic ladder works because each line is a reasonable progression and 'It's the best thing' as the pinnacle of argument is both funny and weirdly sincere. The character voices (earnest Evan, blunt McLovin) work well here.

jokes.text: You changed your name to McLovin? / That's so cool. / Thanks. / So, like, what's Hawaii like?
jokes.setup: A party girl has seen McLovin's fake Hawaiian ID and is treating the fake identity as genuinely cool.
jokes.punchline: 'That's so cool' applied to changing your name to McLovin — and then 'What's Hawaii like?' treating the fictional backstory as real — is a perfect ironic beat. McLovin's fraud is working on the most credulous possible audience.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying payoff to the McLovin fake-ID plot — the ID is finally 'working' because drunk party girls are extremely credulous. 'What's Hawaii like?' is a great button because it demands McLovin improvise an answer to a question he's completely unprepared for.

jokes.text: It's green beer. For your information.
jokes.setup: Seth is trying to get Jules to drink his alcohol by calling it green beer — apparently trying to make it sound special.
jokes.punchline: 'For your information' appended to 'It's green beer' — delivered as if this clarification settles all objections — is a great character beat. Seth believes adding 'for your information' makes this more persuasive.
jokes.explanation: The 'For your information' is the joke — it's Seth performing confidence while being completely transparent in his desperation. The character specificity is high; this is exactly how Seth tries to sell things.

jokes.text: No, that's how I roll. That's the thing. It's no problems. You'll learn that.
jokes.setup: Jules is thanking Seth for bringing drinks to the party; Seth is trying to play it cool.
jokes.punchline: 'You'll learn that.' — delivered as if Jules will come to understand Seth's generous nature over the long term of a relationship that doesn't exist — is perfect Seth delusion.
jokes.explanation: 'You'll learn that' implies a future that Seth has already mapped out in his head — a future Jules isn't aware of. The gap between Seth's vision of the relationship and reality is the entire joke. Good economy and strong character integration.

jokes.text: I love talking and conversing with you. / But I can't hear you, though, because the music is so loud.
jokes.setup: Seth is trying to have a romantic moment with Jules, telling her how much he loves their conversations.
jokes.punchline: Jules revealing she literally couldn't hear anything Seth just said — the earnest declaration of connection was delivered to someone who physically couldn't receive it.
jokes.explanation: Perfect cringe structure — Seth's earnest romantic confession was entirely unheard, making his vulnerability both funny and somewhat poignant. The contrast between his investment and her obliviousness is well-constructed.

jokes.text: Watch your step. I fell earlier today. / Oh, shit. Careful. / Well, I was hit by a car. It's a long story.
jokes.setup: Seth and Jules are heading outside; Seth warns her about the step.
jokes.punchline: 'Well, I was hit by a car. It's a long story.' — the casual dropping of a vehicular accident as context for his step-warning is a great absurdist non-sequitur. 'It's a long story' is the button that makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: Strong callback payoff — the running gag of the cops hitting people with their car pays off here with Seth's completely casual disclosure. 'It's a long story' as his comment on being hit by a car is the perfect Seth energy: everything is a story he'll tell, nothing is actually important.

jokes.text: Are you okay? / I so flirt with you in math.
jokes.setup: Seth has presumably stumbled or done something embarrassing; Jules asks if he's okay.
jokes.punchline: Jules responding to 'Are you okay?' with 'I so flirt with you in math' — a complete non-sequitur that reveals she's been wanting to say this for a while and has found her opening — is an excellent misdirection.
jokes.explanation: 'I so flirt with you in math' is a great line — 'I so' as a construction is funny, and the specific location (math class) makes it feel real. The misdirection from 'are you okay' to this confession is structurally clean. This is a surprisingly sweet and funny moment that lands because Jules is also drunk and sincere.

jokes.text: Tell me about it. I... Samesies.
jokes.setup: Jules has just made a sweet romantic confession ('I so flirt with you in math'); Seth tries to match the energy.
jokes.punchline: 'Samesies.' — Seth's attempt at a romantic response collapsing into this absurd word — is a perfect deflation. He starts to say something real, then retreats to 'Samesies.'
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. 'Samesies' is a perfect coinage — it's what a teenage boy says when he wants to be romantic but can't access the vocabulary. The structure is excellent: he starts with 'Tell me about it. I...' which builds expectation for a matching romantic confession, then 'Samesies' — one word — demolishes it perfectly. High quotability because the word is both funny and true to character. The economy score is near-perfect because nothing could be funnier than exactly that word in exactly that moment.

jokes.text: I've wanted to get with you, like, so hard.
jokes.setup: Seth has just told Jules she's the best girl; Jules responds with her feelings.
jokes.punchline: 'I've wanted to get with you, like, so hard.' — the 'like, so hard' construction applied to romantic feelings is funny because of how it fuses teenage vernacular with sexual directness, and the repetition of 'Like so hard.' as a tag line doubles down.
jokes.explanation: Good final beat — the 'so hard' repetition is funny because Jules is clearly drunk and her verbal filter is gone. The inarticulate directness of teenage desire expressed this way is both funny and endearing. A good ending note for the reel.

jokes.text: "I know, we made some kick-ass tiramisu earlier. It was deli... It looked weird. But it was delicious."
jokes.setup: McLovin is in bed with an older girl who tells him she's never been with an older guy. He responds as if he's experienced and suave.
jokes.punchline: He pivots to bragging about tiramisu — a completely non-sexual, domestic accomplishment — mid-hookup, with an earnest endorsement of its flavor despite its weird appearance.
jokes.explanation: The tiramisu non-sequitur is perfectly in character for McLovin — a 17-year-old fake-ID nerd who has no idea how to behave during a hookup and defaults to listing his competencies like a resume. The structure is tight: the expectation is he'll play along with the romantic/sexual framing, the punchline is a confident pivot to dessert. 'It looked weird. But it was delicious.' is a genuinely funny addendum that extends the joke without over-explaining it. High character integration because only McLovin delivers this.

jokes.text: "Evan. Evan, I'm so wet." / "Oh, yeah. They said that would happen in health, when I learned about it."
jokes.setup: Becca says something sexually suggestive to a nervous Evan.
jokes.punchline: Evan responds not with reciprocated desire but with a clinical reference to health class, as if he's confirming a textbook fact rather than engaging in a romantic moment.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly captures Evan's core character contradiction: he wants this but is so nervous and earnest he retreats into academic language. The health-class callback is a brilliant character beat — he's literally recalling a lesson to process what's happening. The structure is clean: Becca is seductive, Evan is a confused student. Only Evan, specifically, says this.

jokes.text: "You have such a smooth cock." / "Thank you. You would too if you were a man. But you got such a smooth chest."

jokes.explanation: Classic Evan awkwardness — he's so flustered he constructs a grammatically absurd compliment. The logic 'you would too if you were a man' is delightfully broken. It's character-specific cringe that lands because it's completely believable from this character.

jokes.text: "I am gonna give you the best blow-J ever... with my mouth."
jokes.setup: Drunk Becca is trying to be seductive with Evan.
