jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the film. The joke structure is elegant: an already awkward sexual statement followed by an unnecessary clarification that exposes Becca's drunkenness while delivering maximum comedic shock. The pause implied by the scene break between 'ever' and 'with my mouth' gives the line a perfect comedic beat. Highly quotable, widely remembered.

jokes.text: "I don't understand why you have to be such a little bitch about it."
jokes.setup: Evan is being gentlemanly and declining to have sex with a visibly drunk Becca, citing his care for her.
jokes.punchline: Becca, the one who's supposed to be protected, calls the considerate guy a 'little bitch' — a complete inversion of the expected drunk-party-movie dynamic.
jokes.explanation: The joke works because the entire scene has been building Evan as the responsible, almost-too-virtuous partner — and then the person he's being virtuous toward snaps at him for it. The inversion is sharp, character-driven, and plays against genre expectation. 'Little bitch' is perfectly chosen for maximum shock from this character in this context.

jokes.text: "I got a boner." / "Good."
jokes.setup: Seth is in a romantic moment with Jules, trying to make a move.
jokes.punchline: His announcement of his erection as if it's a status update, met with Jules's one-word flat affirmation, is a perfect comedy-of-awkwardness two-hander.
jokes.explanation: The two-word exchange is a masterclass in economy. Seth's blunt declaration is very Seth — no filter, no smoothness — and Jules's 'Good.' is the perfect deadpan response: not romantic, not enthusiastic, just pragmatic. Maximum funny per word. The rhythm is impeccable.

jokes.text: "Do you have a condom?" / "Yes. And lube."
jokes.setup: Jules asks Seth practically if he has a condom.
jokes.punchline: He confirms, then volunteers the lube — an overshare that reveals he came preposterously over-prepared for a scenario he had little realistic hope of achieving.
jokes.explanation: The word 'lube' as a one-word addendum is a beat-perfect escalation joke. The structure is clean: expected answer (condom), then unexpected bonus item (lube) that reveals Seth's pathetically optimistic preparation. It's distinctly his character — over-eager and oblivious.

jokes.text: "Are you crying?" / "No, I just have something in both my eyes. I don't cry. That's funny."
jokes.setup: Seth has just had his romantic dreams crushed when the party gets broken up, and Jules notices he looks upset.
jokes.punchline: He denies crying with an increasingly implausible excuse ('both my eyes') then adds 'I don't cry. That's funny.' — the last line being especially good because it's his lame attempt to frame crying as an absurd impossibility rather than admit vulnerability.
jokes.explanation: 'Something in both my eyes' is a funny escalation of a classic denial, and the meta-commentary 'I don't cry. That's funny.' is a revealing character beat: Seth's ego can't even process his own emotions. Very him.

jokes.text: "I thought we'd both be drunk. / What does me being drunk have anything to do with it? / You'd never get with me if you were sober. Look at you."
jokes.setup: Seth tries to explain why he needed Jules to be drunk for his romantic plan to work.
jokes.punchline: He explicitly says she'd never get with him sober while gesturing at her as if she's objectively out of his league — a crushing, honest, self-deprecating confession delivered without full self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: This is funny because it's both a joke and a genuinely sad moment of self-awareness from Seth. 'Look at you' — gesturing at Jules as evidence of her attractiveness — is the comedic button on a line that's also a character revelation. The joke earns its laugh because it comes from real character truth.

jokes.text: "Drop the crantini and move it, sister." / "See you, sugar tits."
jokes.setup: The cops are clearing the party — a situation calling for authority and professionalism.
jokes.punchline: They deliver orders using absurd frat-bro language ('crantini', 'sugar tits') that completely undermines their authority while revealing how much they've been enjoying the party.
jokes.explanation: The gap between official cop duty and the casual fratty language is the joke. 'Sugar tits' as a farewell from a police officer is exactly the kind of absurdly inappropriate cop-buddy behavior this film has been building. Solid if not exceptional.

jokes.text: "I assume you all have guns and crack."
jokes.setup: Officer Michaels is clearing teenagers out of a house party.
jokes.punchline: He announces his 'assumption' that all the teenagers have guns and crack — a completely disproportionate accusation delivered as if it's a reasonable working hypothesis.
jokes.explanation: A quick, punchy cop-absurdist line. The disconnect between the suburban house party context and 'guns and crack' is the joke. Good economy, though not particularly original in the larger cop-comedy genre.

jokes.text: "Okay, everyone... prepare to be fucked by the long dick of the law."
jokes.setup: Officer Slater dramatically enters the party to clear it.
jokes.punchline: He delivers what he clearly thinks is an epic one-liner — a crude sexual metaphor for law enforcement authority — with full commitment, completely unaware it's bizarre.
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable cop lines in the film. The image of Slater rehearsing this line in his head is funnier than the line itself, which is exactly the character comedy gold the cop subplot delivers. High quotability — it's become a memorable film line. Well-constructed absurdism with specific character voice.

jokes.text: "I'm gonna save you. I'm gonna save you, Evan."
jokes.setup: The cops are clearing the party and Seth dramatically declares he'll save Evan.
jokes.punchline: The grandiose declaration followed immediately by Seth physically struggling with Evan's weight ('Fuck. Fuck, man, so heavy') undercuts the heroism completely.
jokes.explanation: Standard deflation gag — big declaration immediately undercut by physical reality. Works because it's Seth, whose self-image always exceeds his actual capabilities, but it's not exceptionally crafted.

jokes.text: "It's in. Oh, my God, it's in."
jokes.setup: McLovin has been trying to hook up with the girl from the party amid chaos.
jokes.punchline: His awed, reverent announcement — 'It's in. Oh, my God, it's in.' — treats losing his virginity with the gravity of a moon landing, delivered as a breathless status update.
jokes.explanation: One of the best McLovin moments. The repetition 'It's in. Oh, my God, it's in.' treats this private moment like a scientist confirming a successful experiment. The language is so innocent and so McLovin — he's not expressing pleasure, he's expressing awe and verification. Extremely quotable, perfectly character-integrated. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in its specificity and delivery.

jokes.explanation: Exceptional cop-comedy writing. The logic 'guiding his cock, not blocking it' is a philosophical inversion that only makes sense in this absurd context, delivered as though it's sage wisdom. The escalation from 'we don't do that' (a reasonable friendship principle) to 'guiding his cock' (completely insane) is perfectly constructed. One of the best lines in the cop subplot. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: "We know you're not 25, man. We're not idiots, McLovin."
jokes.setup: The cops have been treating McLovin's obviously fake ID as legitimate this entire time.
jokes.punchline: They reveal they knew all along — which recontextualizes all their previous behavior as deliberate rather than gullible, while also being funny because they waited this long to say it.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback that reframes the entire cop storyline. The 'We're not idiots' is funny because empirically their behavior has suggested otherwise, and the reveal adds a new comedic layer to everything that came before. Earns rewatch bonus because earlier scenes read differently with this knowledge.

jokes.text: "When we saw you in the liquor store today, we just... I guess we saw a bit of ourselves, you know... and we just wanted to show you that... you know, cops can have a fun time too, you know?"
jokes.setup: The cops are giving McLovin a sentimental speech about why they befriended him.
jokes.punchline: The gap between the heartfelt framing ('we saw a bit of ourselves') and the actual content (they just wanted to party) is the joke, culminating in the bizarrely modest claim that they wanted to prove 'cops can have a fun time too' — as if that's a profound insight.
jokes.explanation: Solid character comedy — the cops genuinely believe they're giving a meaningful speech, which is the joke. 'Cops can have a fun time too' as a philosophical mission statement is funny but the buildup slightly dilutes the punchline.

jokes.text: "Also, I'm... I'm really sorry that I blocked your cock."
jokes.setup: Officer Michaels is giving McLovin a sincere apology speech.
jokes.punchline: He adds the cock-blocking apology as a formal addendum to his heartfelt speech — treating 'I blocked your cock' as a specific grievance that required its own line item in the apology.
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff on Slater's earlier philosophy. 'Also, I'm sorry I blocked your cock' as a formal element of a sincere apology speech is funny because of the tonal collision — heartfelt apology language applied to a ridiculous subject. The 'Also' is the key word — it means he itemized this.

jokes.text: McLovin suddenly becoming aggressive — 'I'm gonna break your glasses, you fucking cop. You can't hold me. Fucking pigs.'
jokes.setup: The cops want to do McLovin a favor. He asks them to fake-arrest him to impress the girl.
jokes.punchline: McLovin commits fully to the act — going from polite nerd to furious tough guy in an instant, threatening to break a cop's glasses and calling them 'fucking pigs', all with zero credibility.
jokes.explanation: The comedy of McLovin pretending to be a hardened criminal is tremendous because we know exactly how soft he is. 'I'm gonna break your glasses, you fucking cop' is a threat that's specifically threatening someone's glasses — the nerd's weapon of choice for intimidation. The escalation of his fake outrage is excellent character comedy.

jokes.text: "Nice mullet, asshole."
jokes.setup: McLovin is continuing his fake tough-guy performance during the staged arrest.
jokes.punchline: He insults one of the cops' haircut — specifically the mullet — in the middle of his hardened criminal act, which is both the most and least threatening thing he could say.
jokes.explanation: The hair insult is funny as an extension of McLovin's performance — it's a nerd's idea of trash talk. Short, specific, and in character. 'Nice mullet, asshole' is a solid throwaway that earns its laugh.

jokes.text: "He's nuts. Well, we caught the infamous Fogell." / "Wait for me on the outside. We were gonna go to Hawaii."
jokes.setup: The fake arrest is wrapping up and the cops are playing along.
jokes.punchline: Slater declares him 'the infamous Fogell' with cop gravitas, then McLovin breaks character to shout a sentimental farewell about Hawaii to an unseen 'Nicola' — a girlfriend the audience has never heard of, apparently dating a girl and planning travel while being 17 and a virgin.
jokes.explanation: 'The infamous Fogell' is funny because Fogell/McLovin is the least infamous person imaginable. 'Wait for me on the outside. We were gonna go to Hawaii.' adds a lovely absurdist layer — a girlfriend named Nicola, Hawaii plans, the whole mythology of a tough guy going to jail, performed by a 17-year-old nerd. The surprise detail rewards audience attention.

jokes.text: "Man, that's gonna get you so much ass."
jokes.setup: The fake arrest performance has just concluded.
jokes.punchline: Officer Slater immediately drops the cop persona to give McLovin a bro-compliment about how much sex the fake arrest will get him — a completely inappropriate thing for an officer to say, delivered as genuine mentorship.
jokes.explanation: Good cop-character moment — the instant tonal switch from officer to bro-advisor is funny, and 'so much ass' is the kind of thing only Slater would say to a 17-year-old he just fake-arrested. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: "Are you carrying me?" / "No, I'm saving you from the cops." / "You saved me?" / "Well, I don't know what you're talking about, but thanks." / "Can I... Should I just walk? Should I walk?" / "Yeah, sure."
jokes.setup: Seth has been physically carrying/dragging a disoriented Evan away from the police.
jokes.punchline: Evan, confused from drinking, accepts 'you saved me' without understanding it, thanks Seth for something he doesn't comprehend, then matter-of-factly asks if he can just walk — which of course he can, he's not incapacitated.
jokes.explanation: Sweet drunk-buddy comedy. Evan's foggy gratitude and the absurdly simple 'Should I just walk?' question works because it deflates the heroism of Seth's rescue instantly. Warm rather than hilarious.

jokes.text: "Sleepover at my house? You wanna come sleep...?" / "Okay." / "Okay."
jokes.setup: After the entire night's worth of chasing girls and the epic journey to get booze, Seth and Evan's night ends with...
jokes.punchline: ...Seth inviting Evan to a sleepover. Like they're 10. And Evan immediately agreeing. The whole adventure collapses back into their core friendship being two kids who want to hang out.
jokes.explanation: One of the most emotionally resonant jokes in the film — 'sleepover' frames their whole epic night as a prelude to the thing they actually wanted: to hang out together. It's funny because it's so innocent and so true to who they actually are beneath the bravado. Economy is excellent — the joke lives in the word 'sleepover.'

jokes.text: "Does your mom still have pizza bagels?" / "Yeah. Lots." / "Pizza bagels."
jokes.setup: Seth has just invited Evan to a sleepover after their wild night.
jokes.punchline: His first priority is pizza bagels — the same snack they'd have asked about at age 10. The delivery of 'Pizza bagels.' as a standalone sentence of satisfaction/anticipation is the button.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the sleepover joke. 'Pizza bagels.' as a standalone closing statement — the ultimate anti-climax after everything — is delivered with quiet wonder that's genuinely touching and funny simultaneously. It's the purest expression of their friendship's real nature. Great economy.

jokes.text: "We're calling you McLovin." / "McLovin." / "Let's do this dance, boys."
jokes.setup: The cop asks McLovin's real name; learns it's Fogell; rejects it
jokes.punchline: "Fuck that. We're calling you McLovin." The cops prefer the fake ID name to the real one — a full endorsement of the fake identity over the real person
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the film's central running gag. The cops formally adopting McLovin as his permanent name is a satisfying endorsement of the identity he created. "Fuck that. We're calling you McLovin." is a good line.

jokes.text: "He's not usually this drunk when he does this... but I think that could make it more cool."
jokes.setup: Officer Slater is about to attempt the donut maneuver while visibly drunk.
jokes.punchline: Michaels acknowledges Slater is drunker than usual for this stunt, then immediately reframes it as a potential improvement — 'I think that could make it more cool' — as if drunk driving a police cruiser is a performance enhancement.
jokes.explanation: The cheerful rationalization of dangerous drunk driving as 'more cool' is funny because it's so earnest. Michaels isn't being ironic — he genuinely thinks this. Good character voice.

jokes.text: Officer Slater crashes the police cruiser — the stunt goes catastrophically wrong
jokes.setup: Slater has hyped up 'the upward-spiraling pigtail' as one of the greatest moves in donut-spinning history, while drunk.
jokes.punchline: He crashes the car. The grandest setup deflates into the most predictable but still satisfying outcome.
jokes.explanation: The crash is the inevitable payoff on the donut buildup, telegraphed but still satisfying as physical comedy. The escalation setup (greatest move ever, drunk driver, pompous announcement) earns the slapstick payoff. Not original but well-executed.

jokes.text: "Don't blow yourself up, asshole."
jokes.setup: In the aftermath of the crash, things are chaotic.
jokes.punchline: Michaels delivers this as casual advice — 'don't blow yourself up, asshole' — as if self-immolation is a live possibility that just needs a friendly reminder. The casualness of the warning is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Good throwaway line. The casual register of 'don't blow yourself up, asshole' — as if this is standard practical advice between colleagues — is very funny. Economy is high.

jokes.text: "Can we shoot at it?" / "I don't know. Can you?"
jokes.setup: In the aftermath of the cruiser crash, there's apparently a fire or smoldering wreck.
jokes.punchline: McLovin asks if they can shoot at it. Michaels responds not with 'no' but 'I don't know. Can you?' — treating a teenager's request to fire a gun at a burning police vehicle as a matter of personal capability rather than permission.
jokes.explanation: One of the sharpest exchanges in the cop subplot. The grammar joke — responding to 'can we' with 'I don't know, can you' (correcting 'may we' vs 'can we') in a context where the more pressing issue is whether a teenager should shoot at a police car — is sublimely absurd. The cop becomes a permissive grammar teacher. It works on two levels and has excellent economy. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: "Can we shoot at it?" / "I don't know. Can you?"
jokes.setup: The cruiser is on fire; McLovin asks if they can shoot at it
jokes.punchline: The cop responds with "I don't know. Can you?" — a grammar-correction non-answer that completely sidesteps the insanity of the situation and implies the answer is yes if he has the skill
jokes.explanation: Deceptively simple but excellently structured. "Can we shoot at it?" expects either yes or no; instead it gets a pedantic grammar correction that simultaneously permits the action by implication. The economy is near-perfect — five words do the work of a much longer joke. The gap between the seriousness of the response format and the insanity of the situation is the joke.

jokes.text: "Listen, and then she said she was gonna give me a blow-J." / "I can't believe she said that to you." / "Man, you have no idea."
jokes.setup: McLovin is debriefing the cops on his sexual encounter, using 'blow-J' — the same term Becca used (a callback to the earlier scene).
jokes.punchline: The cops respond with the earnest disbelief and admiration of two friends hearing a wild story — treating McLovin's account of Becca's drunken proposition with the reverence of locker-room legend. 'Man, you have no idea' is McLovin's first real display of sexual swagger.
jokes.explanation: The continuation of the 'blow-J' callback is nice. McLovin saying 'man, you have no idea' is a character growth beat packaged as a joke — he's finally playing the experienced guy role. The cops as his audience of admirers is funny contextually.

jokes.text: Seth and Evan's prolonged 'I love you' exchange — escalating declarations of bromantic love between two drunk teenage boys
jokes.setup: Seth and Evan have survived the night and are walking home together. Seth has just carried Evan from the party.
jokes.punchline: What begins as a sincere 'I love you, man' escalates into an increasingly passionate, repetitive declaration of love ('Why don't we say that every day?', 'I wanna go to the rooftops', 'We should go up on my roof') that's simultaneously sweet and deeply funny in its intensity.
jokes.explanation: The sustained 'I love you' escalation works because it's genuinely earned — the whole movie is about this friendship — and the comedy comes from the gap between how intensely Seth is expressing it and how normal it actually is for best friends. 'I wanna go to the rooftops' is a beautiful peak of the escalation. The scene's length (scored here as one sustained moment) slightly reduces economy.

jokes.text: Seth and Evan wake up next to each other — the implied reaction beat as they process having fallen asleep together
jokes.setup: Seth and Evan had a long, emotionally intense conversation about love for each other.
jokes.punchline: The scene cut to morning implies they fell asleep together after all that declaration. The 'What the fuck?' reaction beat on waking is the comedic payoff — they apparently cuddled/slept together as the final expression of their bromance.
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural payoff on the love declaration sequence. The cut to morning and the 'What the fuck?' implies they ended up sleeping together (platonically but awkwardly), which is the comedic culmination of all those declarations of love. Visual comedy from context — the audience fills in what happened. Economy is excellent: the punchline requires no dialogue.

jokes.text: "You wanna hang out? I was gonna go to the mall. I have to get a new comforter. For college."
jokes.setup: It's the morning after the entire epic adventure. Seth is talking to Evan.
jokes.punchline: His morning-after pitch for hanging out is a trip to the mall to buy a comforter for college — the most domestically mundane possible follow-up to their wild night. The 'For college' as a clarifying addendum is funny.
jokes.explanation: Gentle anti-climax humor — after everything, they're going to the mall. The 'For college' addendum is a small funny beat. Functions as scene-setting more than pure joke.

jokes.text: "Cool. So... your mom's got huge tits."
jokes.setup: Seth has just had a sweet exchange with Evan where they implied forgiveness and hanging out. The tone is warm.
jokes.punchline: He punctuates the tender moment with 'your mom's got huge tits' — delivered with casual conversational finality, as if it's a logical conclusion to what they were discussing.
jokes.explanation: Perfect tonal whiplash. The casual insertion of 'your mom's got huge tits' into a warm, reconciliatory conversation is a quintessential Seth move — he can't sustain sincerity, so he punctures it. The 'Cool. So...' setup mimics normal conversational transition before delivering the non-sequitur. Very economical and very character-specific.

jokes.text: "Those are too tight. Way too tight. You need to upgrade." / "But when I was wearing your dad's pants... I realized that if I wear pants that are a little too small it might encourage me to lose weight. And also, chicks can kind of see, like... you know, the borders and outline of my dick a little."
jokes.setup: Seth is trying on pants at the mall after the previous night.
jokes.punchline: His explanation for wearing too-tight pants reveals two completely incompatible theories: weight-loss motivation AND dick-outline visibility. The fact that he's thought this through, including wearing 'your dad's pants' as a trial run, is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Classic Seth logic — a plan that involves both self-improvement and showing off his genitals. The 'your dad's pants' detail is a funny image. The dual-justification structure (lose weight / show dick outline) is well-constructed and utterly Seth.

jokes.text: "Yeah, man, they go nuts for that. The male camel toe." / "Yeah, the camel tail. It's right..." / "I know where it is, where it happens."
jokes.setup: Seth has described his pants strategy for showing the 'outline' of his anatomy.
jokes.punchline: Evan attempts 'camel tail' as the male equivalent of 'camel toe' — the anatomical logic being sound but the term being funny, and Seth cutting him off with 'I know where it is, where it happens' as if this is well-established territory he doesn't need help locating.
jokes.explanation: The 'camel tail' coinage is a funny bit of improv-style wordplay. 'I know where it is, where it happens' is a funny defensive response from Seth — he's both proud and possessive of his own anatomy. Solid crude humor.

jokes.text: "It's like three. It's like ball, dick, ball. It's like a division sign. Like a bunch of people crammed into a van."
jokes.setup: Seth has been describing how tight his pants are.
jokes.punchline: He runs through three rapid-fire metaphors for the arrangement of his genitalia — a division sign being the highlight — building in absurdity with each comparison until he lands on 'people crammed into a van,' which makes geometric but no visual sense.
jokes.explanation: The division sign metaphor is genuinely clever — the mathematical precision of '÷' applied to male anatomy is unexpected and funny. The escalation from division sign to 'people crammed into a van' is a good absurdist leap. Seth's matter-of-fact delivery of increasingly strange comparisons is excellent character comedy. Highly original for the genre.

jokes.text: "Do alcoholics get hangovers?"
jokes.setup: Seth and Evan are at the mall the morning after their big drinking night.
jokes.punchline: Seth asks whether alcoholics get hangovers — the implication being he's so hungover he's pondering whether alcoholism might be a lifestyle improvement. The question reveals he's in serious physical distress and his brain is not fully operational.
jokes.explanation: Five words that do a lot of work. The logic implies Seth is considering becoming an alcoholic as a hangover cure — the implied reasoning is funny and very Seth. Good economy, strong character voice.

jokes.text: "Holy shit, holy shit, holy shit. It's them." — Seth and Evan spotting Jules and Becca at the mall
jokes.setup: Seth and Evan are shuffling through the mall in a painful hangover state, in ratty clothes, holding a comforter.
jokes.punchline: They immediately encounter Jules and Becca — the two girls they humiliated themselves in front of the night before. The 'holy shit' escalation before the reveal is a good beat.
jokes.explanation: Standard sitcom 'of all the places' coincidence setup. Works in context but it's a purely structural move to get characters together — the comedy is in what follows rather than in this moment itself.

jokes.text: "I don't remember anything. So weird. Nothing." — Jules and Becca comparing notes on how much they don't remember
jokes.setup: Jules and Becca are having a morning-after conversation with Seth and Evan, who are terrified of what the girls remember.
jokes.punchline: Both girls independently confirm they remember nothing — which both relieves the boys and reveals the entire traumatic night was lost to alcohol. The mutual 'nothing' is funny as a gift to the audience (and the boys) — the humiliations are erased.
jokes.explanation: The amnesia resolution is a standard comedy trope but it works here because the audience has seen exactly how bad those nights were. The relief and awkwardness of the boys trying to figure out how much the girls know is well-played.

jokes.text: "I didn't puke on you, did I?" / "You didn't. I remember that you... I avoided it. It whizzed right by me, and I said, 'Stay away from me.'"
jokes.setup: Becca, embarrassed about the night before, asks Evan if she vomited on him.
jokes.punchline: Evan confirms she didn't, but his description — 'it whizzed right by me' and 'Stay away from me' — reveals she did in fact vomit, just at him rather than on him. His athletic dodge of her vomit is played as a point of pride.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Evan had to dodge vomit is funny, and his matter-of-fact recounting ('whizzed right by me') as if he's describing a near-miss in sports is good character comedy. The specificity of 'Stay away from me' as his in-the-moment reaction is a nice detail.

jokes.text: "That looks terrible." / "Yeah." / [pause] / "You look great. You don't look terrible. It's just, like, a bad bruise. Everything's great, just from he... This, just like right there. Your eye. Everything else is great."
jokes.setup: Becca has a black eye from the night before. Seth says 'that looks terrible' about it.
jokes.punchline: He then immediately tries to walk it back and digs himself deeper — 'You look great. You don't look terrible' contradicts 'That looks terrible' which he literally just said, and his backpedaling specificity ('Everything's great, just from... this, just like right there. Your eye. Everything else is great.') makes it worse.
jokes.explanation: Classic Seth social disaster — he identifies something, says the wrong thing, then makes it worse trying to fix it. The hedge 'Everything's great, just from he... this, just like right there. Your eye.' is a perfect example of someone talking themselves into a hole in real time. Very true to character.

jokes.text: "On the upside, I think you look cool with a black eye. I'm just gonna throw that out there. I don't... I don't know."
jokes.setup: Seth has been awkwardly backpedaling on calling Becca's black eye 'terrible.'
jokes.punchline: He attempts a recovery with 'I think you look cool with a black eye' — a compliment that only works if you think black eyes are cool, then immediately qualifies it into oblivion with 'I'm just gonna throw that out there. I don't... I don't know.'
jokes.explanation: The continuation of Seth's social disaster. 'I'm just gonna throw that out there' is a phrase Seth uses to disavow responsibility for his own opinions immediately after stating them. The self-undermining 'I don't... I don't know' is perfect — he talked himself into and then out of a compliment in one breath.

jokes.text: "Well, thank you, smart guy. Thanks. That's actually why I'm here. Because I have to get a ton of cover-up for the grad photo."
jokes.setup: Seth has just told Becca she 'looks cool' with a black eye.
jokes.punchline: Becca's dry 'thank you, smart guy' is the perfect deflation, followed by the reveal that the reason she's at the mall is to buy makeup to cover the black eye for her graduation photo — the consequence of the night's events showing up in a mundane, permanent way.
jokes.explanation: Good dry response from Becca. The grad photo detail is a nice comedy-of-consequence beat — the night's chaos has a lasting photographic record. 'Smart guy' is a well-deployed bit of sarcasm.

jokes.text: "I mean, you kind of owe me."
jokes.setup: Jules is asking Seth to come help her buy cover-up for Becca's black eye.
jokes.punchline: She notes he 'kind of owes her' — the casual understatement of 'kind of' applied to a situation where Seth caused her party to get raided by police and caused chaos all night is a good dry line.
jokes.explanation: The understatement of 'kind of owe me' for Seth's night of disasters is a quick effective line. Good economy and delivery.

jokes.text: "Yeah, definitely. I would love to do that. I had such bad acne last year that I pretty much became, like, an expert on the stuff."
jokes.setup: Jules asks Seth to come help buy cover-up makeup.
jokes.punchline: He agrees enthusiastically, then immediately volunteers that he was an expert on cover-up due to severe acne — an unexpected TMI that reframes him as someone with deep personal experience with concealing face problems, rather than a cosmetics consultant.
jokes.explanation: Classic Seth oversharing — he's so eager to be helpful that he reveals a personal vulnerability as a credential. 'I had such bad acne' as the basis of his makeup expertise is both endearing and funny. Very much him.

jokes.text: "Well, you drove. Evan drove me here, though, so..." / "Well, so... Well, I mean, I have my dad's car. So I could just give you a lift... and then Evan could take Becca home. If that works. I don't know if it's in your route."
jokes.setup: Seth and Jules are figuring out logistics so they can spend time together.
jokes.punchline: Seth's flustered over-qualification — 'I don't know if it's in your route' — while trying to arrange a date without calling it a date, combined with the elaborate logistics of separating two friend-pairs, is a funny picture of teenage romantic incompetence.
jokes.explanation: More Seth social fumbling, but slightly over-extended. The logistics scene works as character comedy but the comedic payoff is mild — it's more charming than funny. 'I don't know if it's in your route' is a sweet detail but doesn't generate a big laugh.

jokes.text: "I have your information. So put her there."
jokes.setup: Seth and Jules are wrapping up their mall encounter, Seth trying to confirm plans.
jokes.punchline: He says 'I have your information' (like a salesman or government agent) and then 'Put her there' (a handshake offer so old-fashioned it's absurd from a teenager) — both phrases are from a different era and register.
jokes.explanation: 'I have your information' and 'put her there' are both hilariously formal for a teenager asking out a girl. Seth's social register constantly misfires and this is a good example — it's the language of a used car dealer, not a 17-year-old romantic.

jokes.text: "So can you honestly help me figure out what kind of cover-up to get?"
jokes.setup: Seth confidently volunteered his acne-based makeup expertise to Jules.
jokes.punchline: Now alone with him in the car, Jules asks if he can 'honestly' help — the word 'honestly' implying she has doubts about his stated credentials. It's a small but effective skepticism beat.
jokes.explanation: A quiet closing callback — Jules's 'honestly' is a gentle puncturing of Seth's confident claim. The film ends on this note of mutual, warm skepticism, which is tonally right. Modest as a joke but lands as a sweet capper.
